will have noticed that I have on the order paper a motion, to come up to-morrow, that when the House adjourns on Wednesday the second of June, 1926, it stand adjourned until Friday the fourth of June, 1926. I believe that the members generally are anxious that we should lose as little time as possible in bringing the work of the session to an end.

maintopic: CANADIAN RED CROSS SOCIETY ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext:
Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 151, to amend the Canadian Red Cross Society Act.
He said:	This bill is introduced, Mr. Speaker, at the request of The Canadian Red Cross Society, which operates under chapter 68 of the statutes of 1909, and the amending act, chapter 13 of the statutes of 1922. The society does not possess legal authority to dispose of any property which it holds, and particularly is not competent to give another party legal title thereto. It is given authority to purchase and hold certain property for the purposes of the society. During the war a number of properties which the society obtained throughout the country increased, and now they are being exchanged or disposed of in the interests of the society. It is proposed under this bill to give the society the power to deal with those properties.

speechtext:
Hon. J. C. ELLIOTT (Minister of Health) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 152, to amend the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, 1923.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, this bill covers an
amendment to section 5 of the act to require that where a retail druggist sells narcotics to a physician, veterinary surgeon, dentist or druggist he must have an order in writing. The object is to check up a little more closely the sale of narcotics by druggists.

The last clause consists of adding the word "prescribe" to bring prescribing within the meaning of the act, some question having arisen as to this.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 153 to amend the Criminal Code.
He said: The first amendment proposes to repeal sections 97A and 97B of the Criminal Code as enacted in 1919 concerning unlawful association. There is also an amendment which has passed this House many times and been thrown out by the Senate-respecting offences against girls. We propose to delete the words "of previous chaste character", and in this form we think the amendment will meet with a better fate. Another amendment is to restore to the crown the right of appeal which involves questions of law alone. This existed prior to criminal appeals being established three years ago, which gave to the convicted person the right of appeal under such circumstances, but took it away from the crown which had had it previously. That bill originated in the Senate. The last amendment is the bill which was introduced by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) regarding scrip issued to half breeds. The House adopted his bill last year and the year before but it was rejected by the Senate. The hon. member has introduced it this year, and in order to give the bill a chance to come before the House I have taken the responsibility for it and inserted it in my own bill.

With regard to the right of appeal may I draw to the attention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) the provisions of section 1014 of the Criminal Code.
On the 'hearing of any such appeal against conviction the court of appeal shall allow the appeal if it is of opinion-(a) that the verdict of the jury should be set aside on the ground that it is unreasonable or cannot be supported having regard to the evidence.
Under that section there is the right to allow an appeal on a question of fact if the verdict of the jury is found to be against the weight of evidence. But the great majority of criminal trials are speedy trials before 'a judge alone, and under that subsection there is no right to disturb the decision of a judge on a question of fact. Under subsection (c) there is the right, however, to allow an appeal on the ground that there has been a miscarriage of justice. This section was copied from the act in England, where all trials are by jury, I understand, and in England it has been the custom to

Senate Bills
confine the application of subsection (c) to jury misconduct or some error in trial procedure. I understand the judges of appeal have found it very embarrassing to interfere with the decisions of trial judges on questions of fact where the trial has been held without a jury. This has been brought to my attention by a justice of the appellate division of Ontario, and he strongly suggests that the amendment be made to section 1014. If I may refer the minister to the proposed amendment, section (a) would read as follows:
That the verdict of the jury or the judgment of the trial court. . . .
The words "or the judgment of the trial court" are added.
Mr.^ LAPOINTE: I will read my hon. friend s remarks in Hansard to-morrow and give careful attention to his suggestion.

Would the minister explain more fully what the two clauses are which are being repealed? He stated that they were clauses against unlawful associations, and I cannot recall just now what their provisions were.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I suppose this would come more properly when the second reading of the bill is moved. As my hon. friend well remembers, these two sections were inserted in 1919, some time after the labour disturbances in western Canada. They give the right on the warrant of a justice of the peace to search the papers of a citizen who is supposed to be a member of an association which would come under that section, and anyone attending meetings of such an association would be guilty of the crime of sedition. These were new clauses inserted in the code at the time of the unrest in this country, and that was the reason given for their adoption. All the labour unions of Canada have protested against these sections, believing that they might be construed as dangerous to themselves. However, I will give a fuller explanation when the second reading is moved.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.	[DOT]

MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister' .* The right hon. leader of -he opposition (Mr. Meighen) asked me -owards the cl«j of last week if I would give the House a statement as to the legislation to be proceeded with this session, and as to whether it was all on the order paper. speechtext: Mr. R. B. HANSON (York-Sunbury) moved the third reading of Bill No. 93, to incorporate The Canadian Dexter P. Cooper Company.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE CANADIAN DEXTER P. COOPER COMPANY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my attention has only now been palled to this bill. I suppose it has been carefully considered by the private bills committee, but I notice that under the bill the company asks the right to sell power not only in Canada but in the United States. I would like to know from the promoter of the bill, who is a good lawyer, what will happen under the terms of the act of 1907 if the government determines not to allow the export of power, if, for instance, the province of New Brunswick determine they cannot export power.

maintopic: THE CANADIAN DEXTER P. COOPER COMPANY
speechtext:
The direct answer to that
in this connection would be that under this bill the power itself will not be generated in Canada, but the storage, nine-tenths of the storage, I should say, will be in Canada, and a new section was inserted in the bill in the Private Bills committee whereby all these matters will have to receive the imprimatur not only of the International Joint Commission but also of the Governor in Council of Canada. The provisions of the Export of Electricity Act have been made to apply to this bill, in the same way as the provisions of the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
I might say for the information of the House and of the minister that the bill was considered at three or four long sessions of the Private Bills committee and we gave that aspect, as well as other aspects of this bill, our very best consideration, and finally we adopted as a new section 16 provisions which will in my opinion at all events absolutely safeguard Canadian interests. If they are not safeguarded I wish the House would safeguard them; but so far as I am aware they are already definitely safeguarded. The matter is left in the hands of the Minister of Public Works with respect to navigation; in the jiands of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries with respect to fisheries; in the hands of the Minister of the Interior with respect to power;
in the hands of the International Joint Commission with respect to the division of power; and finally the approval of the Governor in Council must be secured before anything is done. Therefore I think we have done all we can to protect Canadian rights.

maintopic: THE CANADIAN DEXTER P. COOPER COMPANY
speechtext: The bill has not been reprinted. Will the hon. gentleman read the clause in question?

maintopic: THE CANADIAN DEXTER P. COOPER COMPANY
speechtext: I understand the bill has been reprinted. The section in question is a new section-section 16.

maintopic: THE CANADIAN DEXTER P. COOPER COMPANY

maintopic: THE CANADIAN DEXTER P. COOPER COMPANY

The bill has been reprinted, I have
a copy of the reprinted bill here. The measure was fully considered in committee, amendments to it were adopted, and its passage was unanimously approved by the committee. Furthermore, as my hon. friend from York-Sunbury said a minute ago, every possible interest has been looked after and safeguarded. No less than three departments of this government are to be consulted, and the International Joint Commission as well. Finally, after all these proceedings have been gone through, the Governor in Council has to give his approval.

maintopic: THE CANADIAN DEXTER P. COOPER COMPANY
speechtext: Have arrangements been made for the Canadian fishermen interested to be heard by the Departments of Public Works and Marine and Fisheries before a decision is given with respect to this matter? If the fishermen are not so represented I am afraid the privileges which they have enjoyed for several generations past will be jeopardized. I believe the House should be very careful before giving this bill its final reading. Certainly provision should be made so that the fishermen concerned may be well represented before the different departments that have to do with this matter.

maintopic: THE CANADIAN DEXTER P. COOPER COMPANY
speechtext:
The suggestion of my hon. friend is an appropriate one. I have no doubt at all that should any difficulty arise when the question comes up before the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, he will see to it that the fishing interests in New Brunswick are fully represented and heard, and that no decision will be rendered before the case has
Dexter P. Cooper Company

been explained to him. I am confident that no decision will be rendered by the various departments concerned until after the interests affected have been fully and completely -heard.

maintopic: THE CANADIAN DEXTER P. COOPER COMPANY
speechtext: Following up what the Minister of Finance has said, may I put this question: Supposing this company had incurred enormous expense in developing this tidal power, would they not insist then on being given an opportunity to export that power, and is the country protected in that respect?

maintopic: THE CANADIAN DEXTER P. COOPER COMPANY
speechtext: They cannot export power unless they are authorized to do so.

maintopic: THE CANADIAN DEXTER P. COOPER COMPANY
speechtext:
Yes, but they
may spend millions and then make a demand to be allowed to export power.

maintopic: THE CANADIAN DEXTER P. COOPER COMPANY
speechtext: That is their own lookout. I have no doubt the company would not expend a very large amount unless they had the assurance that they would be in a position to exercise the powers conferred by this bill. However, as I have already said the company cannot do anything contrary to Canadian interests without first putting their .case fully before this government, and also before the International Joint Commission, I do not think any hon. member need be apprehensive that Canadian interests will not be fully protected.

maintopic: THE CANADIAN DEXTER P. COOPER COMPANY
speechtext:
There is. one point to which I should like to draw the attention of the House. Undoubtedly, it seems to me, the fishing and navigation rights, and the rights of riparian owners, are safeguarded in the bill. But there are certain new rights with regard to the development of water-powers by means of tidal waters that do not appear to me to be quite so fully guarded. With respect to these new rights, there has not as yet been any judicial expression.
In connection with water-powers developed on Dominion lands, it has been usual to have a clause inserted by which, after the expiration of a certain period, the Dominion government may expropriate the works and regard them as for the general welfare of Canada, provision being made, of course, for the reimbursement of the owners for the outlay they have made. It seems to me that there ought to be a clause along this line inserted in the present bill. We do not know as yet whether there is much prospect of this particular undertaking being a success. We have had no evidence of that from any engineer other than the promoters; but if the scheme of developing electricity 
from tidal waters should prove feasible it may mean a great deal to the future of Canada. Now, I have no desire to enter into a controversy as to whether these waters come directly under provincial or under Dominion jurisdiction, the lawyer members of the committee were inclined to think they came under provincial jursidiction; but I would submit, as a layman, that already the Dominion has certain rights in these waters. The navigation rights of the Dominion are admitted, the fishing rights of the Dominion are admitted, and why should not the Dominion also claim rights with regard to the generation of power. A new right is being created as to which there has been no definite allocation, and I should like to see inserted a clause to the following effect:
The property in and the right to the use of all tidal water ipowers situated within the Dominion of Canada are hereby declared to be vested in and shall remain in the crown; and every undertaking hereunder is hereby declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada.
Unless there is some real objection to this being inserted, I should like to have it adopted as an amendment to the bill-if we have the right to do that in this House. It seems to me that something of the kind is necessary at this stage to safeguard the. rights of the people of Canada.

Now certain work will be Canadian and certain work will be American, and included in the later category is the power site itself. It is next to inconceivable that Canada as a Dominion would want to expropriate half of the work, and especially the half that does

not work. It is the other half that does the work. "The high contracting parties agree that at is expedient to limit the diversion of waters from the Niagara river so that the level of Lake Erie and the flow of the stream shalil not be appreciably affected. It is the desire of both parties to accomplish this object with the least possible injury to investments which have already been made dn the construction of power plants on the United States side of the river under grants of authority from the state of New York, and on the Canadian side of the river under licenses authorized by the Dominion of Canada and the province of Ontario.
So long as this treaty shall remain in force, no diversion of the waters of the Niagara river above the falls from the natural course and stream thereof shall be permitted except for the purposes and to the extent hereinafter provided.
The United States may authorize and permit the diversion within the state of New York of the waters of said river above the falls of Niagara, for power purposes, not exceeding in the aggregate a daily diversion at the rate of twenty thousand cubic feet of water per second.
The United Kingdom, by the Dominion of Canada, or the province of Ontario, may authorize and permit the diversion within the province of Ontario of the waters of said river above the falls of Niagara, for power purposes, not exceeding in the aggregate a daily diversion at the rate of thirty-six thousand cubic feet of water per second.	.
The prohibitions of this article shall not apply to the diversion of water for sanitary or domestic purposes, or for the service of canals for the purposes of navigation."
Whereas, official engineering reports of both governments show that about ninety-five per centum of the flow of the Niagara river passes over the Horseshoe falls, largely on the Canadian side of the International boundary line; that the erosion caused thereby is rapidly changing the contour of the Horseshoe falls 
and is threatening the ultimate destruction of its scenic beauty unless the flow over the falls is lessened and remedial works are constructed to spread the flow of the waters at the crest of the Horseshoe falls;
Whereas, the limited amount of the waters of Niagara river permitted by Article V of the Boundary Waters treaty to be diverted in both the United States of America and in the Dominion of Canada from Niagara river from above the falls of Niagara for power purposes, have already been wholly diverted and utilized in the generation of hydro-electric .power, the demand for which is increasing in the province of Ontario more rapidly than the same can be generated and supplied to its customers by the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario, rendering necessary the early resort to steam generated electric power, unless Article V is promptly amended to provide for a greater diversion of the waters of Niagara river from above the falls of Niagara;
Whereas, the utilization of the waters of the Niagara river provide the most expeditious, efficient and economical source of electric energy in the Dominion of Canada, whereby to supply its municipalities, citizens and industries with cheap electricity which is one of the most important factors in the public, private, social, economic and industrial development of this Dominion;
Whereas, the diversion of the waters of the Niagara river from above the falls can safely be increased to a total of eighty thousand cubic feet per second without the installation of remedial works, and such increased diversion will tend to lessen the erosion and to prevent the anticipated "Suicide of Niagara", and so to preserve the scenic beauty of the cataracts and rapids, a still greater diversion with more favourable results being pehnissible provided the interested governments shall determine on the remedial works to spread the flow of the waters above the crest of the falls;
Whereas, the government of the United States of America has intimated its willingness to conduct negotiations with the United Kingdom through this Dominion of Canada further to protect and preserve the natural and scenic beauty of the falls and rapids of the Niagara, which can only be accomplished by amendment of Article V of the Boundary Waters treaty; and
Whereas .this government recognizes and acknowledges the urgency of co-operative action with the government of the United States of America to the end that the splendor of the cataracts of Niagara may be protected and preserved and the imperative electric power needs of the Dominion may be supplied.
Now, be it resolved: that the parliament of Canada should instruct and authorize the Honourable, the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, to communicate to the proper officials of the government of the United States of America the willingness of this Dominion to discuss the advisability of amending article V of the Boundary Waters treaty, proclaimed May 13, 1910, with reference to an increase m the amount of water permitted to be diverted on each side of the international boundary from the Niagara river above the falls for power purposes and in reference to the joint construction of remedial works for the protection and preservation of the scenic beauty and splendour of the cataracts and rapids of Niagara.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, this motion went
on the order paper on January 8, of this year, and I discovered at that time that the government were giving the subject matter consideration; therefore the motion has stood

Boundary Waters Treaty
over till the present time. Now, with the approval of the Premier of Ontario I want to introduce it for the consideration of the House, as I think it is, without exception, one of the most important matters affecting the people of Canada and particularly t'he people of Ontario. The privy council have recently decided in a case affecting the province of Quebec and important matters bearing upon provincial rights, that it is clear that the province of Ontario and the state of New York jointly own the waters at Niagara falls. It is not, of course, a navigation question, it is purely a power question, with which is mixed up the scenic beauty of the falls, under a former treaty with the United States.
Now the water-powers of this country are day by day becoming of more vital importance than they were in the early stages of our history because of our knowledge of what can be done with electric energy. The great province of Quebec has probably the largest power interests in the world. On the St. Lawrence river, within fifty miles of Montreal, they have within their jurisdiction about
2,700,000	horse-power, and this and other water-power developments within that province are of great provincial and national importance. Sometimes I am sorry that the Dominion does not own those vast resources, which would go far to pay oS the national debt.
As soon as you get beyond the boundaries of Quebec you have on the one side the province of Ontario and on the other the state of New York. It has I believe been decided legally that one-half of the water-power on the St. Lawrence belongs to the state of New York and the other half to the province of Ontario. At Niagara falls the same situation exists. The vital importance of this matter and its relation to section 5 of the treaty is self evident. Section 5 is not affected by any other section of the treaty, nor is it affected by any dispute which has arisen or might arise under the treaty generally. Section 5 merely deals with the property of citizens of the state of New York and of Ontario. Any amendment of that section under the laws of this country is under the jurisdiction of the Dominion of Canada, and of Great Britain as representing Canada in dealing with the government at Washington with respect to treaty matters. But I know the government of Canade are fair to the province of Ontario; that they are prepared to protect the interests of the province and are acting in concert therewith.
Now whatever disputes may arise under the act, if there are any, I want to call attention
to the fact that section 5 is not one with which we should concern ourselves at the moment. The state of New York for over three years has been trying to get the government of the United States to take action. In order to show the position of that state,
I should1 like to read a few extracts from a speech made by the Hon. S. Wallace Dempsey, Chairman of Rivers and Harbours committee, before the mayors of the cities of the state of New York at Buffalo, June 14, 1923. I think these extracts will be considered of great national importance because in my humble judgment they express a fair and proper view of this question and also of the friendly relationships that must and should exist between Canada, Great Britain and the United States. Mr. Dempsey said:
The development of such water as can be diverted from the falls, at Niagara, without impairment of its natural grandeur, is one of the most important of the water-power development problems confronting the country. The question is not alone one of conserving the limited coal supply of the country, but it involves as well the transportation question, which is pressing for solution and becomes acute whenever we have prosperous times, with good crops and factories running full time.
However, as has been saud, the development of our water-power is one of the most important factors in the solution of the very serious transportation problem which now faces us and is bound, with the prosperity and growth of the country, to become more acute before it is solved.
Two hundred and twenty-six thousand cubic feet per second come down the Niagara to the falls. Canada and the United States have agreed, by treaty, to divert 56,000 cubic feet per second for power purposes-36,000 on the Canadian side, and 20,000 in this State. The cataract is divided into two falls

the American, between the American shore and Goat Island, and the Horseshoe or Canadian falls, between the island and the Canadian shore. ' The visitors who view this world's wonder find that the American fall is 1,000 feet wide and has an ample flow of water over its entire width. He learns, on the other hand, that the Canadian or Horseshoe falls is about 3,000 feet wide and sees that a great portion of -that width has a very shallow supply of water, "being for broad widths, nearly bare; that the fall is horseshoe in shape, with almost the whole of the vast volume of water flowing over it at the centre of the horseshoe, and that this concentration of water, with its force and power, is rapidly wearing away and impairing the beauty of the falls. Yet the American falls carries only 10,000 cubic feet per second, while the Canadian falls has the enormous volume of 160,000 cubic feet per second. If the flow of water was spread on the Canadian falls, as it is on the American falls, over the entire width, to cover its 3,000 feet stretch, the Canadian falls would need only three times as much as the American falls, or 30,000 cubic feet per second, to give it ample water and conserve the entire beauty and grandeur of the falls, and corrective works can be placed on .the river, at a reasonable cost, which will spread the flow of the water over the Canadian falls and make a flow over the entire 3,000 feet just as the 1,000 feet of the American falls is covered. Allowing 30,000 feet per second for the Canadian falls and 10,000 additional
Boundary Waters Treaty

to insure against any (possibility of miscalculation, we -could 'have, after deducting this 40,000 cubic feet, the
10.000	cubic feet which fall over the American falls -and the 56,000 cubic feet now diverted for power purposes, 120,000 c.s.f. remaining, which can be diverted without any injury whatever to the falls.
This calculation was made three years ago, 'but the calculations recently made by American and Canadian engineers with a view of finding out what really can be done show
3.600.000	horse power available to the two countries.

speechtext: Under whose instruction was this report prepared?

subtopic: DIVERSION OF WATER FROM THE NIAGARA RIVER AND REMEDIAL WORKS
speechtext:
I understand it was prepared for the governments of the province of Ontario, the Dominion of Canada and the United States. I have not seen these reports personally but I am taking these statements, and those going into the matter will have to verify them. I am not an engineer, but the average given me by engineers is ten tons of coal to an electrical horse power, which means that instead of a saving of 24,000,000 tons of coal there would be a saving of 36,000.000 tons. I am told that coal is worth about $10 per ton, which means that about $360,000,000 is going to waste yearly. Taking it from another point of view, the
3.600.000	horse power belongs equally to the United States and Canada, and we are losing half that amount of money yearly or about $500,000 per day. Mr. Dempsey goes on to say:
This water-power is an all year round power, the most dependable and the best water-power in the world. It can be developed and furnished at the lowest cost per horse-power. And, froan this 120,000 cubic feet, we can develop practically four million additional horsenpower, the equivalent of twenty-four million tons of coal-1/125 of all the coal mined in the United States.
It lias been shown that this power can be developed without lessening, but, on the contrary, heightening the grandeur and beauty of the falls. This power can be furnished the consumer at a much less rate than he can generate from coal. The average cost of power generated from coal is, at the present price of coal, $60 per horse-power, and water-power can be furnished from Niagara to the people of our state at half that price. The demand for power is growing rapidly and steadily, and -it must be supplied either from coal or from water-jower. Should we not then bend every energy (to see that a new treaty is enacted without delay, so that our people may be furnished with this cheap power; that the railroads may be relieved by this one development of carrying 1/125 of their present total tonnage; and the farmer and manufacturer be given the benefit of this carrying capacity to market the products which he has produced; that the demand upon our coal mines may be lessened to this very great extent and the likelihood of a coal shortage or famine be greatly lessened, and that we may, by reducing to this appreciable extent, the demand for coal increase, in some measure, the chances of reduction in the price of coal?

While this next extract is perhaps not relevant, I think it is a proper thing to read now. In his remarks Mr. Dempsey says:
The question of the diversion of water for power, at Niagara, is only one of the many great questions now pending and which will constantly arise between the two countries. If the two countries are to prosper, if they are to have their legitimate growth and development, they must settle the questions that arise between them in an amicable, equitable, give and take way, each remembering that an unconscionable or unfair advantage obtained at one time is sure to be in the mind of her neighbour and may be retaliated many fold when a new question between them must be settled	
The negotiations for a permanent treaty should be undertaken immediately. All that is necessary is the bringing to the attention of the Departments of Foreign Affairs of the two countries the situation as it exists and how easy and immediate the remedy can be. In doing this, the action of just such bodies as that which is in session here will be invaluable. To lessen out transportation problem, to help make our coal problem less acute, to lessen the cost of manufacturing-in consequence, the cost of the manufactured product to the consumer and the cost of living-and to make the state of New ^or^ and the province of Ontario even more desirable places in which to live than they are to-day. I urge that this association bring this matter of the increased diversion to the attention of the State department of the United States, leaving it to act as, with the relations and conditions between the two countries, shall be best and most likely to bring a quick and favourable termination of the negotiations.
I have a number of quotations which I do not intend to read, but I think this opinion, given bjr a distinguished minister of the United States government, might fairly be taken to explain the reasons why prompt action should be taken. I would like to give an extract now from an article written by Mr. Herbert Hoover, Secretary of Commerce of the United States, on Government and Power Development, appearing in the English Review at page 786 et seq:
The real purpose of all this development will be not to make self-satisfying statistics or to provide means for insurance of new stocks and bonds. Its real purpose will be this: That through more power we shall make a still greater saving in labour, shall increase the product of labour, and shall lessen the burden upon labour. Thus we shall gain in higher standards of living, and in wider enjoyment and comfort to every fireside-a goal which should be the sole end and purpose of the economic effort of every nation.
The new vista in progress which has been opened to us is due to the perfection in transmission of electric energy up to 200. or even 300 miles and to higher 'mechanical efficiency of our generators, with capacities reaching up to 70,000 horse power in a single machine. With these twin developments comes the opportunity to generate power in much larger and more economically located stations and to harness and bring to the centres of population water powers which were too remote for use even ten years ago. . . .
When the energy can be supplied in the form of electricity and delivered over a wire, and when the supply is equally available in country and city, there

Boundary Waters Treaty
will no longer be occasion for the crowding we now deplore. . . .
The indirect results, both human and material, are more important than the preceding statements would imply; for no account has been taken of the vast losses to industry and to commerce by the actual 'interruption and threatened interruption of fuel suppQies to our several hundred thousand independent steam units, no account of the relief to shippers from already overburdened transportation and terminal facilities, no account of the increased production of factories from cheaper power, no account of the reduction in physical labour, and the increase in comfort.
To secure the rapid adoption of these demonstratedly possible results is of profound public importance.
The last extract I will read is a short statement from the report of the New York State Power Commission to the legislature of the state of New York, which body approved of the report, made in 1924:
A revision of the treaty on boundary waters for the purpose of securing an increase in tihe amount of water that may be diverted from the Niagara river for power purposes, is urged by the commission, inasmuch as it is provided in any plan for increasing the amount of diversion to safeguard the scenic beauty of the fa-lfls.
The full amount of water permitted t(T be diverted from the Niagara river on the American side has been utilized since July, 1922. At the present time, a large addition to the steam plant of the Buffalo General Electric Company is being made for supplying the increased demand for current in western New York. Current generated at the falls is sold at prices below the prices for current produced by steam.
The development of energy from an increased diversion will make available down the years a large amount of power which may be furnished at a cheaper rate than steam produced power.
In 1910, when this treaty was made, there was very little known about power production. The Niagara Falls Power Company, which was in existence then, had 100,000 horse power, and only used 100 feet of fall. To-day the Hydro-Electric Power Company have a fall of 315 feet, and whereas the old company develops only 10 horse power to the foot, the Hydro-Electric Company develops 35 horse power to the foot fall, so it can readily be seen what a vast change has taken place. The United States has passed legislation that no longer could a company proceed to get power for any length of time if they only took the 100 foot drop. . They have to get all the power out of the water available at the falls, and the only company to do that today is the Hydro-Electric Power Company. They have not enough power. It is quite current in our papers that Canada has 36,000 second-feet, and the United States only 20,000 [DOT] second-feet. When that treaty was made, the United States had two power companies in Canada shipping power into the United States, and that power came out of that 36,000 second-feet belonging to Canada. So that ever since the treaty was made the United
States has been getting more power from Niagara Falls than Canada. That, of course, was a matter of arrangement. We used only about 3,COO horse power when the treaty was passed.

So far as this Niagara Falls question is con-erned, it is not a new one. Sir Adam Beck, when he ibuilt that famous hydro plant of his- and it is the best in the world-bought enough land on one side of where the water comes from, that is from Chippawa down to Queenston, to build another plant just as big, and that right of way has been in existence now for four years. I am told that he was trying during his lifetime to get some agreement made through the government of Canada with the United States so that he could get more power at the falls, but whatever the reason of the refusal may have been, it looks now as if the two countries were getting together on this matter, which is of the greatest importance both to the state of New York and the province of Ontario.

The state of New York, and twenty-one states altogether, are behind tho American government in the legal battle with Chicago. There are ten states down south that are fighting with Chicago. The case is now before the Supreme Court of the United States, and it is for that court to decide, but why the province of Ontario and the state of New York should not have their own power properly developed is something I cannot understand; I cannot see the logic of it. The state of New York is fighting our battle. They need power just the same as we do, and the state of New York will be entitled to one-half of whatever we get. I think the province of Ontario should get what belongs
Boundary Waters Treaty

to it, and the state of New York should get what belongs to it.
I have perhaps spoken too long on this matter. I have a feeling that if the engineering statements are correct-and I believe that the best engineers we can secure and the best engineers the United States can secure are right-it is obviously a national crime to both countries for the present state of affairs to continue. The people of this generation in the state of New York and in the province of Ontario, and perhaps elsewhere in Canada and the United States, should have the use of this 3,600,000 horse power a year, or, if you like to put it that way, of this 36,000,000 tons of coal. This power can be produced probably cheaper than any other power that now remains in the world, except, perhaps, the power on the St. Lawrence. Taking the cost of the coal at S10 a ton, it means that we are throwing away $360,000,000 a year through not using this power, or about $1,000,000 a day. That does seem foolish, or crazy, if you want to put it that way, because this is power to which every man and woman in Ontario and Quebec and every man and woman in the state of New York are entitled to have the benefit of. This power belongs to the state of New York and to the province of Ontario, and its development will cheapen production in the state of New York and in this province for every man and every woman in that territory. In the words of Mr. Hoover, it would be a national crime if we did not as soon as possible see what changes can be made. The engineers have admitted that the scenic beauty of the falls can be preserved for all time. It will not longer be committing suicide, as Mr. Hoover describes it, to use this power. The front portion of the Horseshoe falls will have to be raised up with asphalt and other material, so that you will have the same level on our side of the falls as on the American side. To retain the scenic beauty of the falls-and it is disappearing at the rate of eight feet a year-you have to raise the level of the water of the Horseshoe falls and if you do not use that water so raised for power purposes you would flood jhe state of New York and the province of Ontario.

This question, Mr. Speaker, is one that is interesting,
I take it, to the whole country. It certainly is of interest to us who live close to the falls. The first thing it strikes me that we have got to do is to preserve the scenic beauty of the falls. What effect will it have upon the falls to make the diversion of water to the extent that the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Bristol) has mentioned? That is not exactly known, but I can say to the House this much: The Parks commission, who have in their keeping the water of Niagara Falls, have been in close touch with this matter for thirty-five years, and I can say this also to the House, that the amount of breaking back of the falls amounts to five feet every year. That takes place at the peak of the Horseshoe falls, and it can be prevented. Not only that, but the scenic beauty of the falls can be preserved and a lot of water diverted to commercial purposes provided we go about the matter in the right way. -
Now as to the method to be adopted for the preservation of the falls and the utilization of the water at the same time, I can say this much further:	Anybody who has
been there will know that the volume of water is in the centre of the Horseshoe falls. All that needs to be done to spread the flow of water over the whole area of the brink of the falls is to provide remedial works of a very inexpensive nature that will stop, or tend to stop to a great extent, the erosion at the centre of the Horseshoe falls. I do not know whose duty it is to carry out that *work, but it is a very important matter. If it be true that you can prevent further erosion and at the same time preserve the scenic beauty and then utilize the remainder of the water for commercial purposes, see what an immense asset you have. For the information of the House I can say that the
10.000	cubic second feet that is being diverted by Chicago would be equal if utilized at Chippawa to 330,000 horse power. That is what Chicago is stealing from us to-day. I ask hon. gentlemen to pause and consider what that means. Now if an additional
10.000	cubic second feet will provide 330,000 or 350,000 horse power at Chippawa on a fall of 315 feet, then twelve times that amount will yield three and a half million horse power such as my hon. friend (Mr. Bristol) has spoken of. One of the members from " Toronto asked how the calculation was made. The calculation is correct; the engineers of the Park commission have compiled the data.
To illustrate further what the Chicago diversion means, all you have got to do is to

Boundary Waters Treaty
visualize a stream of water three times the width of this chamber with a depth of ten feet. That will enable you to realize what Chicago is stealing from this country. In the face of that is it any wonder that lake Erie, lake Huron, and the other lakes, are being emptied of water? Something must be done in this matter without further delay. I have been a member of this House for a number of years and whether we are getting anywhere on this question I cannot say; but I realize that nothing effective is coming from any protest we are making: Chicago keeps on taking the water, and the level of the lakes continues to fall. We have noticed that the water of lake Erie, for example, is going down at the rate of six inches a year. I happen to belong to a shooting club that had shooting and fishing rights at Port Rowan on lake Erie, and during the last three years the water on the marshes there has receded 32 inches. Just imagine a situation of that kind. I only mention it to illustrate what happened on these lakes. It will not be long before this government will have to spend thousands upon thousands of dollars in order to keep the inland harbours of this country open.	.

I have no complaint to make
about any of the statements made by the hon. member for Toronto East Centre (Mr. Bristol) or the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin). The matter of developing increased power at Niagara is receiving our very active consideration. I was delegated by this government to go to Washington a short time ago and discuss the matter with the Secretary of State, and may I say that all our negotiations with respect to this and other international matters are carried on directly with the Washington authorities. While there I discovered that there is a wish there to discuss the whole problem.
The hon. member for Lincoln has spoken of the lowering of the lake levels. The hon.
member for Toronto East Centre has discussed not only the lowering of the lakes but also the Chicago diversion. While the latter question incidentally plays some part in the matter it ought not to be a factor in delaying the completion of an understanding about the power development at Niagara. That is a point I wish to make, and it is [DOT] one I urged very strongly at Washington. I pointed out that this question was vital to the province of Ontario for the reason that the Chippawa power plant is advantageously located for the distribution of power throughout central and southwestern Ontario, and the development of increased power there would be beneficial to the power users of the province. Furthermore a great deal of money has been spent in developing the Chippawa plant, and they are getting the highest efficiency out of the use of the water there, perhaps higher than anywhere else in the world. For that reason we want the full concurrence and assistance of the Ontario government in whatever steps we take. I may say that we have kept them very thoroughly informed as to every move we are making in connection with this matter.
On going to Washington I found that the American authorities were particularly concerned about the preservation of the scenic beauty of the falls, taking the ground that that must be the first consideration-with which we agreed-and that before there was talk of diversion that problem must be taken up and satisfactorily settled. Needless to say, that will be solved by the better distribution of the flow of water across the face of the falls, which will prevent what the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) has just pointed out, the rapid rate of erosion, withr out endangering the scenic beauty, and will permit a further utilization of the flow of water in addition to that already in use. But that is a question that will be settled by the investigation which is about to take place.
May I say for the information of the House that we have named Mr. Biggar, the Chief Electoral Officer, to go to Washington, meet representatives of the government there and discuss in detail the investigation that must take place-first as to the preservation of the scenic properties of the falls, and secondly as to what further amounts of water can be diverted.

Then what is the use of these farmers being induced to grow sweet clover or fodder corn, or some other kind of fodder crop, unless a profitable market can be found for the cattle which are to be raised on that feed. In many parts of western Canada we are now troubled with what is called soil drifting. This land has been farmed for several years for the raising of grain crops almost exclusively. To prevent this soil drifting we are advised to grow fodder crops so as to get the grass roots back in the soil. I think that is very necessary. At the same time we must have some profitable way of using the crops which are so grown.
I do not wish to take up much of the time of the House in connection with this subject, but I think I have presented enough facts to convince hon. members that something should be done to help this industry if a way can be found to do so. I think the best way to discuss this matter is in a small committee; it is very difficult to do it in a House composed of 240 members. I am now only going to suggest very briefly how the industry may possibly be helped, and I hope that a committee of the House will be appointed which will deal with the matter. We are faced with an exportable surplus of cattle of, I think, between two hundred thousand and three hundred thousand head. I did have the figures here but for the moment I have mislaid them. Can we increase the consumption in Canada so that this total surplus may be eaten here? I think it cannot be done at the present moment at any rate; we must export quite a percentage of our cattle crop. The two principal export markets which we have to-day are Great Britain and United States. I find that we are practically shut out of the United States by a tariff of l\ cents per pound on cattle weighing less than 1,050 pounds, and by a tariff of 2 cents a pound on cattle over that weight. Then we have a freight rate from Calgary to Chicago of about $13 per head. The tariff of 2 cents a pound on a 1,200 pound steer amounts to $24. That is we have to pay $37 to get a steer from Calgary into Chicago. Then with respect to our other market, Great Britain, we find that the total freight rate from Calgary to Britain,

Cattle Industry
according to information which is given in a government bulletin here, is $50.79 per head. It seems to me that in the case of both these markets there is a very fertile field for investigation by a committee to determine whether some relief might foe secured for the cattle industry. For instance, I find that the feed for a steer from Montreal to England costs $4.50 per head. It is quite possible that might be reduced. The ocean freight is $20 per head. It is possible that some arrangement might be made whereby that might be reduced. I also notice in the booklet already referred to that the department itself is suggesting the possibility of co-operative shipments to the Old Country. I should like the committee to-carefully investigate that matter and see whether, through some assistance rendered by the federal government, it might be possible to ship cattle co-operatively to Britain. I was told recently by a friend of mine that a neighbour of his had sold some cattle last fall before making a trip to England. He sold one steer in particular for $25. He afterwards engaged on a cattle boat going to England and assisted in feeding the cattle on board. While on the way across he found that this animal which he had sold was one of the stock on the boat. He took the trouble to see some of the steers sold in the Old Country, and although he failed to see his own particular steer sold he observed animals which were very similar in weight and conformation sold for $125 per head. Now the freight over is about $50, and he had secured for the steer $25, a total of $75. But the steer apparently brought in Great Britain approximately $125. If the man who raised the steer in Alberta could have secured that other $50, or even one half of it, it might have encouraged him to stay in the business. It is possible that the committee which I am asking may suggest means by which a part of this spread may be retained for the producer.
I do not want to say very muhh about the United States tariff against our cattle, but I notice that the Financial Post of a recent date had a front page article regarding the benefit of the United States market to Canadian beef cattle. According to the press there is a wish at the present time on the part of a large number of farmers in the corn belt of the United States that the American tariff against Canadian cattle should be lowered or removed. I think that this matter too might be carefully considered by a committee to see whether anything should be done by Canada to co-operate with these United States farmers in an endeavour to secure a reduction of
the tariff. I may point out that the great loss which our cattle men suffer-and which I am sure hon. members will realize by the figures I gave at the opening of my remarks-wa3 largely occasioned by the fact that the United States in 1921 placed an emergency tariff of 30 per cent against our cattle. The following year that duty was changed to the rates I quoted a moment ago, namely li cents a pound on cattle weighing less than 1,050 lbs, and two cents a pound in the case of cattle over that weight.
It should be pointed out that for a period of six or seven years while the United States had cattle on the free list Canada maintained a duty of 25 per cent against cattle coming from the United States into Canada. Mr. Tom King, of Washington, D.C., addressing the Western Canada Live Stock Union in December last, said that in his opinion, if they wished to secure free entry for their cattle into the United States it would be necessary that Canada should grant to the United States the same concessions in regard to the tariff on cattle as we hoped to get from the United States. We must have reciprocity in the matter. I am not going to suggest to this House what should be done. I will simply bring the matter to the attention of the House, and if the committee is appointed I think this point Should be carefully discussed by that committee.
Before closing I desire to give to the House the opinion of the Western Canada Live Stock Union and the request they are making to the members of parliament. Possibly all hon. members have received this request and I will simply read the last three or four sentences:
That Canada oould, if the master were to receive the attention it should, negotiate for the modification or removal of this tariff.
That is it improbable that this (tariff ever would have been put in iforce with respect to Canadian cattle if there had been a Canadian representative at Washington.
We therefore earnestly ask for your active assistance in securing a modification or the domination of this tariff, thus removing this handicap from the cattle industry of Canada.
We would also ask for your interest in securing the appointment of a Canadian representative at Washington, and we believe that when appointed, such representative should be familiar and an sympathy with the live stock industry. Such a representative could be of inestimable service to Canada.
It seems to me that the plight the industry is in, the hard years it has gone through, make it unnecessary for me to speak at any greater length in support of the request that a committee should be appointed to inquire into

the industry and report to parliament any measures that in their opinion might conduce to the benefit of the industry. I ask hon. members of this House to give their support to this resolution.

speechtext:
I can scarcely let this resolution, with which I have so much sympathy, pass this House without saying a few words. Permit me to congratulate the hon. member (Mr. Coote) on his effort in placing before the House the position and needs of the live stock industry, the most important and basic industry in western Canada. It is important because you must have live stock on the farm to produce fertility and to keep the soil and the crops from deterioration. The live stock industry plays an essential part in this feature. The hon. member who introduced the resolution has covered the points pretty well. There are many things of importance pertaining to the live stock industry which come vividly before us. I have appealed to the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) and I have appealed to the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) to try to get him to reduce the rate on live stock to Great Britain, but up to the present I have failed Many promises have been made but there has been no action. They say it is impossible to convent the government merchant marine vessels into cattle boats, on account of their construction. However, I have my doubts about that statement. I have shipped on the Canadian government boat Victor and several other boats, and found them splendid cattle boats. If the Jensen boats could be converted into cattle carriers, I do not see why the Canadian Government Merchant Marine vessels could not be made available for the carriage of cattle, and thus relieve this industry. A statement was made before toe Railway committee on Friday that the Jensen line was in the hands of a receiver. That is not the case. Mr. Teakle, the manager of the merchant marine I understand made that statement. The boats of the Jensen line were changed in Germany, and in connection with the changing of the boats some dispute arose. The price for the changing of them was to be based on the Clyde estimate, and not on the price fixed in Germany. I understand from the owners or the men who had to do with the Jensen line that the money is waiting in Toronto to pay for the remodelling of the ships. I have asked the government for a 815 rate on cattle and I am about through 
with it. I do not think I will bother the Minister of Railways or the Minister of Agriculture any more. I am not speaking for my own purposes at all, but I am making a plea for the industry. Here we are with a market in Great Britain clamouring for our live stock. There are men the Old Country prepared to buy thousands of cattle. But we have had nothing but promises from the minister. Every time the Minister of Agriculture goes west, he says, "We will give you redress," but so far he has taken no action. I have finished with my appeals to the minister. I cannot make any impression on him and I have done my duty to my constituents.
Here we are in Canada with a dwindling industry. We are shipping 100,000 cattle as the hon. member for Macleod has said. Ireland is shipping a million and the Argentine shipped 1,285,000 cattle as dressed beef. They are shipping those into Great Britain.

speechtext:
I am going to talk kindly to the minister because I want to make a few converts. Ireland ships a million cattle, Ireland contains 32,605 square miles, Manitoba 255,832 square miles and Canada 3,745,674 square miles. Canada ships a paltry 100,000 cattle when we should be shipping a million. There are lots of cattle in the country. Canada has wonderful possibilities, particularly in the agricultural line. The Minister of Railways knows something about what this industry used to be in the early days, but it has been dwindling every year, because no encouragement is given to it. When you commence to talk to anyone about the cattle industry, he will say, "Get out of the way, I do not want to be bothered with you." But the day will come when people will be bothered with us. Our shipments of cattle are dropping every year and soon they will be at a vfery low figure.
As to the question whether Canada should go into the live cattle industry or the dead meat industry, I say the only hope for Canada is in the live stock and shipping industry. It is absolutely impossible to ship dead beef, and I make that statement after fifty years experience. I tried the experiment of shipping dead meat and suffered losses. The dealers in Ireland want us to get out of the business and to make way for them. In effect they say, "Don't come over to the Old Country with your Canadian steers which are of such a superior quality." I have stood in the Glasgow market and have sold a hundred cattle while the Irishman has been left standing at the rail with the same number. That

Cattle Industry
is due to the stamina, the admirable quality of the Canadian steer as a feeder. I saw Canadian steers eating 112 pounds of turnips a day in Scotland. Anyone who knows anything about the live stock industry knows that a country that goes in for raising live stock is a wealthy country. If you come with me to Illinois or Iowa I will show you a rich country. Scotland, the north of England, or any other country that is in the live stock industry is prosperous and doing well.
As regards shipping dead meat the Argentine Republic ship great quantities of dead meat into the Smithfield market where it is sold for 4 to 41 pence per pound. I have a quotation which came to-day of Canadian cattle selling at 11 pence per pound. What do hon. members want? Do they want to ship dead beef at 41 to 5 pence per pound or do they want to ship live cattle and get into the 11 penny market. The minister through his department tried an experiment in regard to dead meat and I think the loss was $50 per head. They tried live cattle and succeeded. Why is it not possible? The Englishman is a connoisseur on meat; he knows the quality. Scotch home-fed cattle are selling at the highest pinnacle in the Old Country; then come the English home-fed cattle; then come your dressed cattle from the other side of the water and last of all comes the Argentine chilled and frozen meat selling for 4-| pence while the better cattle get the higher prices.
I would not advise anyone to ship yearling steers because nowhere in Canada have we as much roughage feed available as we have in western Canada and in western Ontario we have similar facilities. We should bring our yearlings up to two years or three years until they weigh about 1.200 pounds and when they have reached 1 200 pounds that is the time to send them to the market.

Mr. Speaker, when the
House adjourned at six o'clock I was dealing with the live stock industry and trying to steer a few of our members in the right course by pointing out to them the absolute imposs:bility of shipping dead beef in competition with our live cattle. I desire to be brief, but this is a subject of such great importance to the cattle industry of the Dominion that I want to bring it before, the House in a very definite form for the last time, as I have spoken of it so often that I feel sometimes I may have been
thought out of place in referring to the subject.	.	_
Canada has taken a foremost place in England with her live cattle. She cannot retain that place by shipping the beef dead; it is an absolute impossibility. At the greatest cattle fair in England, the Norwich fair, a Canadian steer took the first prize. But there are those in the British Isles who seem to want to get Canada out of the live cattle industry into the chilled meat business; in fact, they are so strongly opposed to the importation of our live cattle that an Irish paper, the Mid-Ulster mail, of September 29, 1923, contained the following article:
Those Canadian "Stores"
At long last the Canadian stock exporters seem to be realizing that in attempting to send store cattle into Great Britain in open competition with Irish stores they are "on a bad egg," and that the removal of the embargo on the importation of Canadian cattle was not, for the Dominion stock-breeder, synonymous with an introduction to El Dorado.
It is now announced in the press that Colonel Mullins, of Winnipeg, who is largely interested in the export of cattle from western Canada to England, has accepted an invitation to attend an agricultural conference in London at the end of December to explain how the present high freights have put business out of the question. Exactly, btit let us not forget that high freight rates are not entirely to blame for the lack of business in Canadian store cattle. From first to last this embargo business has been a "stunt"-in Canada worked by the politicians, and in England by some sections of the press. Cattlemen in the Dominion who understood their business never wanted the embargo raised, for the very good and sufficient reason that Canada can put meat on the British market for 3d a pound less as chilled beef than when the animals are imported alive into this country.
Several shipments of Canadian cattle have been landed in Britain this year, but in the majority of eases the animals have not been "stores." They are practically fat cattle, and some of them had even been specially fed in Canada so that when they arrived they would create a good impression among British cattle buyers. When consignments of real Canadian "stores" arrived the animals were in many cases practically unsaleable, being considered too old and too rough to repay the cost of finishing in the fields of the Mother Country.
It is evident that Ireland desires to divert Canada into the chilled beef line of business. Now I do not want to see this country make that mistake and so let the Irish cattle breeders have a monopoly of the store cattle market in Great Britain. The prices in England to-day are very high, lid. per pound, while chilled beef is selling at from 41d to 5d. Lord Bledisloe has become a convert to the purchase of Canadian cattle. At one time he was our absolute enemy, but he has purchased 100 Canadian steers and placed them on his grass. England wants as many cattle as we can send; we have an unlimited market

Mr. Speaker, in addressing the House on this resolution, namely:
That, in the opinion of this House, a special committee should be appointed to examine into the whole situation of the cattle industry with power to recommend any measures that in their opinion might conduce to the benefit and further development of the industry.
let me say, that the words of Horace Greeley are as true to-day as they were the day they were uttered, when he said: "At the head of all science and art, at the head of all progress and civilization stands, not militarism, the science that kills, not commerce, the art that enriches, but agriculture, the mother of all industry and the maintainer of human life.'' This is an expression which we in Canada might well take to heart, and we might well consider it at this present time when we are discussing the possibilities of this country, because we know that when agriculture in Canada is prosperous it follows that every other industry will naturally be prosperous. That fact has been brought home to us very plainly during the last twelve months, as the result of the splendid harvest and the splendid success which has attended our agricultural operations throughout the length and breadth of this Dominion.
We have heard a great deal said on the floor of parliament this session, and a good deal from our hon. friends opposite, respecting the keeping of the boy on the farm. It has been amusing all through life to me to listen to these fellows, some of whom have been born on the farm, and who are now engaged in other walks of life, turning and telling us that we should do everything possible to keep the boy on the farm. It reminds

"Stick to the farm," said the president To the wide-eyed country hoy,
Then he hied him away to his White House home With an air of rustic joy.
"Stick to the farm," said the railroad king To the lad who looks afar,
Then he hies him back on the double quick In his rustic private car.
"Stick to the farm," said the clergyman To the lad on the worm fence perched,

I am not one of those who would say to our western farmers, or to the young man who comes out from the Old Country and goes to our western prairies: You must at once engage in live stock lines. Not at all. These men have to do as circumstances will permit them, nevertheless, if we are going to make agriculture as successful as it ought to be, if we

everything he requires in the matter of raw material at the lowest possible cost.
I have often heard it said by hon. gentlemen: "Oh, I would not treat with the American people at all." What are the conditions? Here we are, two friendly nations, living alongside of each other, with two artificial tariff walls' built up by each country against the other, and yet in the face of those walls, out of a total foreign trade of 2,255 million dollars we are doing over 1,095 million dollars' worth of business, almost one-half the entire trade of the country, with our American cousins across the border. Does that fact not prove how anxious these two people are to do business, the one with the other? Trade is not a national business. Trade is an individual matter, and if a Canadian buys anything across the line he does so for one reason only, and that is he thinks he can get better value for his money by purchasing there than he can get anywhere else in the world. If an American does any business in this countiy it is for the same reason. Therefore, I repeat, to such a degree do the people of the two countries realize that they can do better trading with each other than with any other countries that nearly one-half our entire foreign trade is carried on with the United States. Is that not at once an illustration of the power of natural trade laws, and an indication of the only rational trade policy? I do hope that as soon as possible we may be able to show the great benefits which will result to both these countries by the following of such a policy to a greater degree than we have been able to do up to the present time.
When we consider the terms of this resolution we find that it embodies another thing. If this is to become a great agricultural country and continue to grow and thrive as it ought to, we must not only encourage a system of keeping live stock but encourage the keeping of the very best class of animals which can be obtained. That is something which, if I wished, I could spend hours dilating upon, because as agriculturists the greatest drawback towards the success of the live stock industry in this country is that those who are engaged in the business do not understand the science of live stock breeding and feeding to the degree to which it ought to be understood. If we did understand and practice the proper system of live stock production we would not see so many of those half-starved animals going into every live stock market from week to week and month to month. To accomplish the best results, a start must be made during the breeding period. Whenever animals are dropped we should realize that the first func-

tion of food is to support the requirements of the animal system, and it is only from what the animal can properly digest and assimilate over and above that which is required to support the animal system that we can derive a profit. Therefore it should be the aim 'of every farmer, of every live stock raiser, so to look after those animals from the moment they are dropped as long as he keeps them in his possession, that when he disposes of them they will be in such a condition that he can get the highest price it is possible to obtain in the best market.
I am not going to continue this discussion at any greater length because there are members to my right and to my left who are able to give us a great deal of valuable information along this line.

That conference was held prior to the sitting of the present congress and these farmers, about a million strong, were preparing their presentation for submission to congress. To-day congress has rejected the only proposition that has been placed before it that would go to help the United States farmer out of the undesirable position in which he finds himself as a result of a high protective tariff in that country. Des Moines, December 22/26.-Representatives of a milibon western farmers issued tiheir manifesto at the dosing session to-day of the conference of the corn-belt committee and the executive committee of the American Council of Agriculture.

Further, more than sixty-six per cent of the people of the United States of America reside in towns and cities and all these people, more particularly those who have not a large income, require the necessities of life as cheaply as possible. For the benefit of Canadian agriculture, if we could only get access to the American market we know there are in the cities of the eastern states more men able to command an annual income of $10,000 a year than are to be found in all the rest of the world. These individuals do not require to consider the cost of living; they are bound to have the best at any price. Canada, on account of her northern climate and her capabilities, on account of the brain and brawn of her people, is able to produce the best goods in the world, and1 if we could secure access to those markets our superior quality of product would displace a great deal of the inferior article produced by the United States farmer to the wonderful benefit of the Canadian farmer. For these reasons, which I have in a few minutes tried to enunciate, it is the duty of this House to see to it if possible that a committee is appointed to make an exhaustive investigation into the whole matter of the live stock industry of Canada with a view of finding some remedy, through the medium of cheaper transportation and better returns, which will enable us to produce more profitably in the future than we have done in the past.

What is proposed in the McNary-Haugen bill, to which allusion has been made? It is not proposed that the United States should do away with protection and become a free trade country; not at all. What is proposed is ^merely to provide a huge sum of 'money, $675,000,000, for the purpose of taking care of the exportable surplus produced in that country. There is no desire among those people in the central states to do away with protection; there is no movement of that kind there. Who is the one outstanding figure in this whole movement? Ex-Governor Frank O. Lowden, of the state of Illinois, and a more staunch protectionist you cannot find either in the United States or Canada or in any other part of the world. The men who are foremost in that movement of the American Farm Bureau Association believe that protection, properly applied, will protect the farmer in the United States just as it will in any other country, and I share that view. Some people have said that a man is a protectionist in his early youth, and again just before he dies, and that in between he is something else. That may be so, but the fact remains that agriculture in this country can, in my humble judgment, be protected, and that protection will give it added assistance and new life. If we have not been protecting it in the past, that is no reason why we ought not to protect it in the future. If we have not been doing the necessary things to create new wealth in the past, that is no reason why we ought not to do them in the future. Some of these things occur to this House from time to time. Others, I believe, could very well be studied by a group of experts in this country. I have not had a chance to examine into all of the studies that Doctor Tory, for instance, has made, but I say to this government and to the last government and to any other government, that if we would utilize one-hundredth part of the intelligence of our universities and of our business men, and of the genius of the people of this country, we would find solutions for a great many of the problems which are now left to drift from session to session.

That 47,000,000 bushels that was imported by Great Britain from Canada may have lived up to the grades at which it left this country. I am not finding fault with that; perhaps that is what the minister refers to. But take the millions of bushels that go through Buffalo and other United States ports, and which are mixed with American grain and then shipped overseas. Surely the identity of that Canadian grain is lost; there is no question about that. So that after all my point is this: A system of education amongst the British people themselves should be undertaken, and in addition to that distribution centres, not controlled by foreign countries, should be established. Because practically every avenue for the distribution of Canadian wheat in Great Britain to-day is a distribution centre which handles wheat from the Argentine and from every other foreign country from which Great Britain makes importa-[DOT] tions. Consequently it is in a position to determine what quantities of foreign wheat shall be handled there, what quantities of Canadian wheat for example, and the price is set according to the world's parity, although it may differ in different months of the year. The subject is a complex one and I state at once that I do not know everything about the problems of wheat. That may be apparent from my remarks, but I also say this: I have given the subject some close study, and I daresay there are many other hon. gentlemen here who have not given it any study at all. I have been interested in the matter because I am trying to find in my own mind some basis upon which we in the east could stand and assist the people in the west. In other words, the application of protection to Canada and the empire as well. If, for instance, Great Britain bought one hundred million more bushels of Canadian wheat and paid 20 cents more a bushel for it, instead of

Is it not reasonable to suppose that under those circumstances the price of foreign wheat in Great Britain might fall 20 cents? I give that to hon. gentlemen as a point to think about.
I believe that the new Self-Supporting League recently established in England, with the object of enlightening the people there as to the quality and value of the various products which are imported into the United Kingdom and sold there, will accomplish a great deal of good, and that the overseas dominions will reap some benefit in this direction. That the embargo on Canadian cattle was not removed for a considerable number of years was due largely, I think, to personal interest somewhere on the other side. If we can harness personal interest in the Mother Country with personal interest in the dominions overseas-with personal interest in Australia, South Africa and Canada-if we can get on common ground in the matter of marketing the products of the far flung portions of this empire, in the heart of the empire, and get a preference in exchange for a preference I think we shall make progress along the line of developing not only industrial life but farming life in the overseas dominions themselves as well as in the Mother Country.
I may tell hon. gentlemen who are interested that if they will get in touch with the secretary of the Self-Supporting League in London they will get from him information which bears the imprimatur of Stanley Baldwin, Prime Minister of Great Britain, along the various lines I have been speaking of. Now I want to make another observation in connection with the very important resolution we are now considering. It is that this government, or any government in power in Canada, can afford to let a great many of our undertakings in the matter of public works, stand for the time, and concentrate their attention and the attention of parliament upon these very important industries, the cattle industry, the agricultural industry, and above all the manufacturing industry. I believe we have got to find new avenues and new methods for the financing of new enterprises in this country, because it certainly will be utterly impossible for anybody to go out among the investing public-certainly no group of men in this House can do it-and get new capital for new industries; they will not be able to sell new preferred stock, or bonds, or common stock in new enterprises, directly the people become seized of the fact that double taxation will have to be paid-that is if that taxation

But I am speaking of new capital for new industry, and it seems to me that in this particular line this government and this parliament has to devise some new method of assistance, in order that we may have new industrial life in this country, new agricultural life and new cattle industry in portions where it does not now exist. I believe it is possible to have t'hiis renewed vigour in a nation devoting itself to that financing and that development through private sources, if you will, or by whatever method may be devised, and we wil find here plenty of attraction for immigrants all over the country, even from the United States. Once we have provided the places to work in, which are infinitely more important than the places to live in, we will have immigration. I
wish to congratulate the mover of this resolution (Mr. Coote) for having presented it to the House.
