There is nothing more
Cattle Industry

important in my opinion in agriculture than the development of the live stock industry and of a mixed system of farming, in preference to a single crop system. I do not criticize or censure the man who settles on a new piece of land where Providence has supplied him with nitrogen, potash and phosphates, which he can help himself to in favourable years. I think he is quite right in getting himself established by securing as much natural wealth from the soil in the early years of his occupation as he can. These products assist him in becoming established. History will repeat itself on the new lands in Canada, as it has done in all parts of the continent of America; after ,a while that stored-up fertility of the soil will become exhausted and he will have to adopt a mixed system of farming, or live as some men do who grow wheat on poor soil in some other parts of the world.
I think it has been clearly shown that we can produce in Canada as high a quality of beef as can be grown anywhere. We have on more than one occasion shipped grass beef from Alberta to the Chicago market, where it has easily topped the market and Obtained a higher price than the American beef sent from the various American states. We have also shipped some of our store cattle over to Great Britain, where they have been prepared and finished by the feeders on the other side, and in competition with the best British animals at some of their most important exhibitions have won the first prize. 'In British Columbia we produce a very 'high quality of beef on our ranges, and I wish to say that the taste of British Columbia bunch grass beef would attract a person under any conditions. We have in that province one of the largest cattle ranches in Canada. Among the various problems we have to meet in the cattle business are first, the production of good quality, secondly, the growing and finishing of those animals, and third, the [DOT]spreading out of our marketing system [DOT] over a greater period of the year. These are problems that can be controlled very largely by the farmer himself. In the first place, he requires to breed properly in order to produce the proper kind of beef; in the second place he must feed that beef liberally during the growing years, and then finish it off to a greater extent on our western plains and on our western farm lands than is being done at the present time. I quite understand that it requires a good deal of skill and perhaps some more expensive appliances in the feeding of cattle, although in the western country those animals feed out in the open, with the light brush found there as a protection,
[Mr. Tolmie.l
do much better than those tied up. In that great country where cheap food is easily secured the feeding of cattle should be profitable.
Another serious fault is rushing the cattle to market during the last three months of the year. I have seen train loads of cattle being sent out to the market at Winnipeg heading from the newer sections of the prairie provinces and these cattle looked as though they were bred for speed rather than for beef. It is no wonder they secured only a small price when they reached their destination.
With regard to freight rates, in a country with such large areas and huge distances the question of rates will always be an important matter in transporting the animals to market, and every effort should be made to lower the freight rates as far as possible. There are many problems in connection with the shipment of cattle across the Atlantic which have to be seriously considered, and the matter of fixing freight rates is not nearly so easy as one might be induced to think after hearing some of the remarks which have been made on this question. Return cargoes have to be looked for and many other things have to be taken into consideration before a solution of the problem can be found.
In regard to the shipment of chilled meat as compared with live beef to the British market, it has been solved long ago. Argentine can beat us in the matter of chilled beef. I was much surprised to find the uniform quality of the Argentine beef in the Smith-field market in London in 1921. The quarters were very similar, well-conditioned and even in quality, and much in demand by those who desired beef that had been chilled or frozen. However, the Britisher is perhaps the best judge of roast beef in the world-and he has not acquired his knowledge in a short time; he has acquired it after hundreds of years. At the time I was there fresh-killed beef was at least 50 per cent higher than the chilled article, so that it is reasonable to say that when the Britisher demands that quality of beef we must pay attention to that particular phase of our export market rather than attempt to make any experiment at the present time.
Again, Argentine is able to produce her beef at a very much lower cost. Therefore when it comes into competition with that beef on the other side our chances of success would not be good.
We have heard the United States referred to on two or three occasions to-night and I am quite sure that anyone familiar with the live stock business will admit at.	*u-t

the United States, situated as closely as it is on the south, is the natural market for our beef. But the people of the United States have something to say about that and we are not going to be able to remove that tariff until they feel inclined to do so and that it is to their benefit to have the tariff removed. The range cattle men of the United States cover a large part of Texas, Arizona, New Mexico, Montana, Wyoming, Idaho, eastern Washington and Oregon, parts of California and Nevada. These men are producing meat under the same conditions as our men on the western prairies. They are looking fo.r a market in the -corn-belt. It is these men who together with many other farmers brought pressure to bear on the United States government in 1920 and brought in the emergency tariff at that time to be followed shortly afterwards by what is known as the Fordney tariff.
Therefore the United States farmers are not inclined to favour the removal of the tariff and I am rather surprised to hear that there have been some large meetings of farmers asking for this. I would imagine they would be largely influenced by the Democratic party. Only a week or two ago I quoted a number of articles from various live stock papers in the United States clearly showing that when the dairy industry was in jeopardy only a few months ago the United States did not hesitate to increase their tariff on butter by 50 per cent. In addition to that, resolutions I quoted showed that they desired an increased tariff on canned meats, hides and some of the other by-products of cattle.
With regard to the British market I think at the present time we might supply animals of better quality. As I said a short time ago better breeding of our live stock and better feeding of these animals during the growing period will, if carried on in this country, have good results in relation to our success in the British market. We are a little short of animals of as high a quality as might be desired and there is some inclination on the part of some shippers to fill out shipments of cattle with animals of an inferior quality. This is not going to help our market in Great Britain. We have established a high standard there and we should maintain it so as to keep Canadian cattle continuously in demand in that country.
Another very important market is the home market and we should produce beef of a better quality. I will never forget attending the annual meeting of the Aberdeen Angus Breeders' Association in the city of Brandon a few vears ago when beef was served from prize steers. This was the finest beef I ever
tasted in this or any other oountry and anyone getting a taste of such beef as that would want as much of the same quality as he could possibly get. One of the reasons why people do not consume more beef in this country is because they frequently get beef of a very poor quality. Just to-night I faced a piece of roast beef that I had to give up after arguing my way through half of it. It was so tough it would drive a hungry man away from a chuck wagon. It is by raising a high quality of beef and putting -it on the market so that it will be more attractive to the consumer that we shall help to build up our home market.
Beef has to face the competition of discarded old dairy cows that have done years of service in the dairy business and that have earned their cost over and over again. When they reach an age when they are of no more profit in the dairy business they are sent to the packing house. If we produce more of a good quality of beef to come into competition with those animals, we can drive them into a can or a sausage casing, which is where they really belong.
We should make every effort to gain entry into Great Britain with our dairy cattle. We have been more progressive than any other country in the world in cleaning up our dairy herds and placing them on a good, sound healthy basis by the use of the tuberculin test. We have developed the producing quality of our dairy animals to a great extent so that they will be in demand in any country in the world. We have on more than one occasion held the dairy record for the production of milk and butter, and after looking over some of the dairy herds of Great Britain I am quite sure they could be much improved by the addition of some good Canadian cattle.
I heard the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan) comparing farming conditions in Canada with those in Great Britain. The farmer in Great Britain is not a pioneer farmer; he is on a farm that has been cultivated for many ears. He is farming land that is under drained, that has probably permanent fences and permanent buildings, and in that way he does not have to invest much money on capital account. In my farming operations west of the mountains I have always found that when I get a little bit of money saved up I have somewhere to put it, such as in clearing land, putting up a fence or new buildings, or draining land. The British farmer has not these things to do and he is consequently aJble to put more money aside where a reasonable profit can be made.
Cattle Industry

I am rather surprised to hear the statement about the United States farmers not desiring a tariff, because as I said a moment ago the government did not hesitate to increase the tariff in the United States on dairy butter once the farmers made an appeal to have that done. With regard to the Haugen bill, which has been referred to on more than one occasion to-night, this had its object, if I understand it correctly, the assistance of the United States congress in finding a market for the surplus products of the fanners of that country. The great objection to this, I understand, is that if a price was set above the normal market prices of the world it would cause a tremendous increase in the production of these particular products with the result that it would be very difficult to find a market for the surplus, and the deficit would have to be carried by the United States government.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for South Huron, who I know is an expert in the breeding of beef cattle, a gentleman whom I met on Farmers' Institute platforms years ago west of the mountains, and who is well known to the beef producers of Canada. I heard him a few minutes ago speaking about the wonderful market in the United States. I quite agree with him. He also referred to
10 p.m. that market of moneyed men in the larger and more populous centres, the men in those centres who would demand a nice thick, juicy steak from a choice steer and who are not afraid to pay for it. In some of the United States hotels it is not uncommon to pay as high as three dollars for such a steak. Let me ask my hon. friend how those conditions were created in that country. How did they get their wealth? Why are those people able to pay those high prices for the products of the farm? This has occurred in a country that has maintained for many years the highest protection in the world. They have conserved for their people the wealth of that country; they have conserved for themselves their own market, and just as soon as we get sense enough to plug up the leak in Canada, to keep our home market for ourselves and keep our young men at home, we shall enjoy our full measure of prosperity.
The hon. member sitting to my right (Mr. Maclean) also referred to a proposal of his to combine the two great railways of Canada.
I have been informed by some of our largest shippers that if there is one thing in the world they do not want it is a combination of these two roads. They said that while freight rates were fixed on the same basis on these two roads, still there was a great deal of competition for the business, which was very beneficial [Mr. Tolmie.3
to the live stock owners, and as a result they got their cars much quicker and in better condition and the animals were handled much more expeditiously to the market than under the old conditions when one railway controlled the whole situation.
I have very much pleasure, Mr. Speaker, in suporting the resolution.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find myself
largely in agreement with the very excellent remarks of the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie). Indeed, I doubt very much if we could work up any controversy over a resolution with the spirit of which most of us seem to be in hearty accord. I think it is generally accepted that we can not have agriculture in a permanent and sound condition without some form of live stock. It will be recalled that after the war probably no line of agriculture was more severely hit by the terrible deflation of 1920 than live stock. Most of us expected there would be a tremendous slump in grain prices, and many farmers thought they would make provision for it by going more largely into live stock, only to be hit at least as quickly and sometimes more fatally than were the grain-growers. It was because of that deflation, and of the further fact that we were shut out of the American market by the tariff and had not yet acquired the British market by the removal of the embargo, that our live stock men found themselves wrestling with three difficulties-terrible deflation of price, exclusion from the American market, and the British market still closed to them. As a result the live stock industry, especially in the ranching country, was struck a staggering blow and for a while we were afraid it would disappear. Since then there been a marked improvement, especially during the last two or three years, not only in the quantity and quality of our live stock but also in prices and profits.
Just a word on the British market.. While it is far away it has many advantages. There are three conditions we must comply with before we can get in there and stay: one is quantity, the next is quality, and the third is continuity of supply. There is a general opinion that if we have a run of cattle in the early spring and another in the fall, that will suit the British market. This is not correct according to my information. That market will take Canadian cattle every week and every month of the year, provided you have the right kind to offer. What we have shipped

Cattle Industry
so far is only a bagatelle required with the aggregate requirements of that market.
Why is it we need more quantity now? It is true that the quantity that is being shipped to-day to Great Britain as compared with 1922, the year before the embargo was taken off, -has increased 500 per cent, and during the same period our shipments to the United States have decreased 230 per cent leaving a slight net gain in the aggregate of our shipments. But why are there not moire? I can remember when almost every farmer of western Ontario had a fine bunch of steers which he turned out for the admiration of the visitor. Down in the Mari times, adjalcent to the bay of Fundy, where the hay barns sometimes are full to overflowing, with the hay market gone and no stock to feed it to, why are they not shipping more beef stockers to the British .market? I wonder if we have lost the desire for the constant work that usually goes with fattening live stock? Or is it because our youths for the most part have left the eastern farms and are doing this work out west? Whatever the reason may be, we have to start over again and build up this industry. Therefore, is it not natural that it should take time, to build it up? For thirty long years this industry with the Old Country was destroyed, and now we have to build it up almost from the bottom. During the three short years we have been able to increase our shipments, as I say, by 500 per cent, though we have to admit during the same time a decrease in our business with the United States of 230 per cent.
The fact that we are deprived largely of the American market has driven us to the overseas market and has had the effect of improving the quality of our stock; because nothing but quality can afford to pay the freight rates for that tremendous distance. To that extent, perhaps, we have benefited. That is to say, the more remote your market, the higher the quality of the goods must be to stand the freight carrying charges. The poorer the quality of your live cattle, the nearer at home you must market them because they will not cany themselves to the distant market. Consequently we have an incidental advantage in the improvement of our stock. I do not take much consolation from that fact, for I should like to have both the American and the British market, but having been deprived of the former, it was nothing but a godsend that shortly after we secured practically free access to the latter. Continuity means that we must be in the business in
earnest, shipping every month of the year, so that those who have gratified their appetite for our cattle can look forward to getting a constant supply.
My good friend from Marquette (Mr. Mullins), whom we always like to hear on the cattle industry, is no milk and water admirer, he is a real live stock man. He may not feed very many live stock, but he understands the game and he is in it heart and money and everything else I expect. But sometimes he makes remarks that may leave the impression that if I chose to do so I could dig up some real cheap freight rates, and could even command the waves. Well, my hon. friend will remember we made a rather futile attempt to do something in the direction of lower ocean rates a year ago. Maybe if it had been made at some other time than what was supposed to be just before a general election, the effort would have been received with some degree of unanimity on all sides. Nevertheless it was a gesture in the direction that my hon. friend desires, and it is to be hoped that in the not too distant future another effort will be made. At all events I think it is required. But under the present method of shipping our co-operative marketing facilities have not reached the stage where they can ensure that boats at -Montreal, Quebec or St. John will be filled shortly after arrival in port. That is the trouble. By actual working out we find that at least in the first two years after the embargo was taken off, 30 per cent of the space for cattle was not utilized. How can we get cheap freight rates when at times only 70 per cent of the space is filled on the return trip? It is a matter of evolution, but our boats at the various ports must be met systematically with our shipments of cattle and practically every space be filled- so that those may earn the fullest possible revenue.
I am not as free to speak as the hon. member for Marquette, but I do not find myself entirely in sympathy with his desire for a cheaper freight rate. I can assure him that there is no great shortage of space at present. His information is that spaces are short and that some of our space brokers in Montreal could place lots of cattle if they had the boats. That is not our information; they have succeeded in concealing that condition from the Live Stock branch. If there is any shortage of spaces I can assure my hon. friend that I would be very glad to know of it, but that is not my information.
Cattle Industry

speechtext:
Is the hon. gentleman
aware that the Welshman, the largest carrier out of Montreal, is laid up, and that the Ionian has been taken off the run, leaving a shortage of ocean space?

maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The actions of these big shipping companies are very mysterious, and I will not pretend to account for them. But at all events there is a tremendous market in England, able to consume anything we are likely to produce during our lifetime. We are now only shipping a bagatelle, but we are trying to encourage the production of cattle in Canada. Cheap rates are being given eastern buyers in order that they may go west to buy cattle, shows are being promoted in the west, and the result is that the feeding of cattle in winter has been stimulated since the British market was opened.
I might just add a word or two to what was said by the hon. member for Victoria regarding the remaining restrictions against Canadian cattle. I do not want to criticize too much; I think we have made good progress, but there are still restrictions against our cows which might be investigated by this committee, and a case might be prepared for the Imperial conference which is to take place some time m October. Representations might be made to the home government to put Canada on a parity with Ireland with respect not only to stockers but other cattle as well. A committee of the English House, after debating this question last year, strongly recommended that no discrimination should be made against one overseas dominion as compared with another in the matter of the shipment of live cattle. That referred to Canada, of course, and our representative was largely instrumental in having that resolution passed.
So much for the British market. I would now like to say a word about the American market. I do not wish to revive the old question of reciprocity with the United States; I do not think it is a live question except to certain individuals. Some day it may come to life again, but just now there seems to be only a hope on the part of Canada that something may be done. This hope is not shared by the hon. member for Victoria; he does not think there is much sign on the horizon that the United States will reduce the duty against our cattle. Nevertheless, in 1923 Right Hon. Mr. Fielding brought down an amendment to the Customs Act, which I would like to read:
If the president of the United States, under authority of the United States Tariff Act of 1922, determines to reduce the duties imposed by such act on the following articles, that is to say:

Cattle; wheat, wheat flour; oats; barley; potatoes; onions; turnips; hay; fish as enumerated in paragraphs 717, 718, 719 and 720 of the said tariff of 1922, the Governor in Council may by order in council make such reductions of duties on such articles imported into Canada from the United States as may be deemed reasonable by way of compensation foY such reductions on Canadian products imported into the United States.
It was then thought that this would constitute a friendly gesture towards the United States in the way of reciprocal relations on these specified products. Speaking from memory I think nothing materialized from that amendment. As the 'hon. member for Macleod pointed out, Mr. Tom King, speaking last winter at a meeting in Saskatoon, drew attention to the fact that we in Canada could not expect to have any particular move made by the government of the United States towards a reduction of duty while we maintained a tariff of 25 per cent against American live stock. For a time our live stock went freely into the United States, before the Fordney tariff was established while we maintained! a 25 per cent duty against importations from that country, and Mr. King pointed out that the first step we should take in Canada was to make it plain what we meant by the term "as may be deemed' reasonable by way of compensation for such reductions on Canadian products imported) into the United , States." In this connection the following order in council was passed by the present government on May 18, 1926:
At the Government House at Ottawa,
Tuesday, the 18th day of May, 1926.
Present:
The Deputy of His Excellency
The Governor General in Council:
Whereas section 80 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1907, as amended by chapter 42 of the statutes of 1923 reads as follows:
"8C. If the president of the United States, under authority of the United States Tariff Act of 1922, determines to reduce the duties imposed by such act on the following articles, that is to say:
Cattle; wheat; wheat flour; oats; barley; potatoes; onions; turnips; hay; fish as enumerated in paragraphs 717, 718, 719 and 720 of the said tariff of 1922, the Governor in Council may by order in council make such reductions of duties on such articles imported into Canada from the United States as may be deemed reasonable by way of compensation for such reductions on Canadian products imported into the United States."
And whereas the time would seem to be opportune in so far as cattle are concerned for the talcing of such action on the part of Canada as is possible, looking toward the freer exchange of agricultural products between the United States and this Dominion: Therefore the Deputy of His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Agriculture, is pleased to authorize and doth hereby authorize and instruct the Minister of Finance to take such action as may be necessary towards the reduction of duties on cattle entering Canada

Cattle Industry
from the United States in the event of the United States reducing the duties on Canadian cattle entering their country, the reduction in Canadian duties on cattle to toe in the same proportion to tihe present duty as the reduction in the United States duty is to the present United States duty.
That is to say, every advance made by the United States government in the way of a reduction in duty on Canadian cattle will be met by a corresponding reduction in the Canadian duty against American cattle. So it will be seen that according to this order in council we have a brick for brick policy; that is to say, every brick the Americans take off the tariff wall against us will be met with the removal of a corresponding brick from our tariff wall against American cattle. There is this outstanding difference between our policy and that of our hon. friends opposite. They usually speak of their policy as brick for brick in a wall that is being built up. Our policy is a brick for brick downwards. I shall not dilate on that except to say that we just as well as our friends opposite, have a brick for brick policy, but ours is brick for brick downwards.

speechtext:
That is the policy of
destruction.

speechtext:
I do not think my
hon. friend will take much exception to this. Exceptions prove the rule, you know. On occasions like this we do not want anything but a real good discusion of this very important question. I do not know that the American people are ready yet, but we will be ready on this side, ready to come downward the moment there is any such indication on the other side.

speechtext:
He is a Canadian
correspondent at Washington and seems to be giving the news for all parties. We see his articles in our press, and he is usually looked upon as a reliable dispenser of news on agricultural matters.

speechtext:
Was he not
representing somebody from the United States when he made those statements in the west?

maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
He might lhave
been, but I have found him a very levelheaded gentleman.
I would judge from the remarks of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) that he had in mind the desirability of securing the American market for our beef animals, our stockers, and such like. I presume he will agree as to the advisability of extending the scope of this inquiry to dairy cattle and breeding cattle.
Cattle Industry

He does not differentiate between them, but simply speaks of the cattle industry. With that in mind, may I say a word with regard to our dairy cattle industry in this country?
We are making good progress, I think, with regard to dairying, especially of recent years, particularly with regard to the export of butter and still more with regard to the quality and quantity of our exports of cheese. Cheese is the standby of the average Ontario farmer. It is to him what wheat is to the western farmer. It is the chief source of revenue of many of the farms here in Ontario. When you look up the statistics and find that the average production of milk per cow in Canada is less than 4,000 pounds per annum, I do not see how some of these cattle are worth carrying over. The production of some runs to twice that amount, and consequently some must run to only half that amount, and with the drag on the industry of a large number of dairy cattle not paying their board, it seems to me that if it was only for that one thing the committee might do a lot of educational work by pointing out, if it be for the one-'hundreth time, the advisability of culling out these animals from our dairy herds. It is distressing. They take up just as much room in the stable, eat practically the same amount of feed as the good producers, and the result from these culls is negligible, and the little bit they do give they are very often unwilling to give, and you have to run around all over the shop after them. I can think of no greater drag on the dairy industry. My hon. friends opposite may blame that on the Australian treaty. I do not think so, even accepting their viewpoint of the treaty. Examine the dairy herds within a certain radius of this city. Go out in the middle of summer and see the calves out in the open, with not a twig to shade them from the burning sun, wagging their little tails off shaking off the flies, wearing themselves out in their infancy- that is the way they are preparing themselves to become dairy cows. It will not do. We have a lot to learn yet.
It is amazing to me that with this disability, and with the further disability of the small cheese factories with their small output per factory, and the consequent higher cost, that we stand top of the ladder to-day in the British market in regard to the quality and quantity of our cheese. We would be several notches higher still, and the farmer would have more profit in his pocket at the end of the year, if we removed these disabilities. A lot of the men with good herds are doing well, but, on the other hand, the man who has only this kind of herd, whose cows 
milk for only six or seven months of the year, who tries to economize on feed in the winter and turns his dairy cattle out in the spring so poor that it takes half the summer to get the old hair off, cannot succeed. I think, therefore, if the hon. member for Macleod will open the door wide enough and have the committee consider the improving of the individual dairy unit, which is the cow, it will be worth while. The improvement of the quality of our dairy products in western Canada has been very gratifying. We have come to it gradually. Someone has said that if you abuse this old earth of ours by bad farming, sooner or later that earth will discipline you, and by climatic or other conditions will compel you to adopt some system of farming that will enrich the fertility of the soil. We are learning that lesson.
I would not presume to speak authoritatively regarding agriculture in the Maritime provinces, but if there is one thing agriculture needs in the Maritime provinces more than another it is live stock, particularly around the bay of Fundy where they have such an abundance of feed and frequently nothing to feed it to. By way of encouraging them, at a number of our experimental farms down there last winter we put on a bunch of feeder steers to demonstrate what could be done in feeding steers and getting them ready to ship to the British market. The Maritimes are right at the front door of Canada, and shippers of cattle in the Maritimes are better off by $19 per head than the shipper of cattle at Regina or Saskatoon We in the west have to pay $19 more freight in shipping our cattle to the British market. They have nothing but ocean transportation, while we have the long land haul with its consequent increase in cost. It is true that^there are other conditions as to which we enjoy an advantage, but I am satisfied the Maritime provinces are starting out on an era of improved agriculture. I had an opportunity of discussing the matter with some of the public men down there, some of the ministers of agriculture, and they impressed me very much with having the right slant on some of the things that are wrong in the Maritime provinces. You can get wheat gliding through their ports on a scale of ten and twenty million bushels if you like; but what you want is something that will develop new wealth and production, and, instead of importing farm products as they are in many cases, exporting them to the markets of the world.
I would suggest to the hon. member for Macleod that he take advantage of an exist-

Cattle Industry
ing committee instead of asking for the appointment of a special committee when we feel that we have just about had a surfeit of special committees this session. We are all looking to the time when this session will close. Prorogation we hope is not too far off in the distance, and instead of organizing a special committee at this time, which would make it more difficult than ever to carry on morning sessions in the course of a week or two, why not take advantage of the select standing committee on Agriculture and Colonization, or some committee that is already constituted? If such committee is too large the question might be referred to a subcommittee. I would have much preferred had this resolution come up for discussion earlier in the session, because there was a long period-three or four months, three months anyway-when the Agricultural committee had nothing to do but kick their heels waiting for something to turn up. That would have been an excellent opportunity, when we were wasting our time in other respects, to have referred the whole question to them. However, that opportunity is past, and it is no use in expressing regret over the fact. But I w'ould suggest that even now the subject would receive more attention from the select standing committee on Agriculture and Colonization than a special committee would be able to give it at this period of the session.
However, whether or not my hon. friend accepts that suggestion I am going to support his resolution. There is no reason why, either at this session or at another session, we should not have a useful discussion on how to improve the live stock industry of Canada. Because it is not keeping pace, not even in the matter of production. There is a popular idea that the question of production does not enter into the problem at all. My experience is that if you have a good export steer it is half sold, there is no doubt about it. But it does not follow that because you get that far you should stop there. The great question of co-operative marketing is still in its infancy in Canada. But the evolution stage is proceeding rapidly from ,one stage of perfection to another, and when the process of co-operation is carried out to its fullest extent with the result of saving the greatest possible amount of time and money, then producers will realize better prices for their animals. It is sometimes asked: What can we do? Well, the situation here is the same as in the case of any other gospel, the gospel of salvation for example, or of better markets. You have got to keep talking about it and pointing out methods of improvement in order to get people to listen.

maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I have listened with much interest
to the remarks made by different speakers on this resolution, and particularly to the remarks offered by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) who would naturally be supposed to be in close touch with the whole question, and in view of the fact that he has been engaged in agriculture all his life would be regarded as having as intimate a knowledge of the whole subject as anyone in Canada. I regret, however, that the Minister has taken his seat without throwing very much light on this much vexed question. It is true he told us that agriculture is on the eve of a great development, that good times are in store for us, and that the government passed an order in council in 1926 offering certain concessions to the people across the line if they would only allow our cattle access to the markets of the United States but no solution of the difficulty is suggested. The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) I observe, has had this resolution on the order paper since January 29, upwards of four months, and as the minister says that in all probability the session will close in the course of a few weeks we may not have an opportunity to go into the matter in detail even though a special committee were appointed.
In closing the minister touched upon the subject of co-operative marketing, a matter which might well have occupied the attention of himself and his department. But so far as I can see the government have been absolutely asleep at the switch in regard to action on their part. It is true that in western Canada something along the line of cooperation has been done during the last year with regard to the marketing of wheat and grain grown in those provinces, and I am quite confident and quite hopeful that good will result from those efforts and that it will blaze the way for other branches of agriculture making progress along similar lines. But in the meantime what has the federal Department of Agriculture been doing in the matter. We are spending upwards of $6,000,000 per year on this department and the head of that department admits to-night that they are not doing anything in regard to co-operative marketing. It is true, he says, there are great possibilities along that line and that we are on the eve of a great era of development, but so far as his own department is concerned, I cannot see that it is doing very much in the way of encouraging development.
The minister says that the average milk production of the dairy cow is below what it should be, that the people are not providing proper shelter for young and growing stock,
Cattle Industry

and so on. It is all very well for the minister to criticize those who are endeavouring to carry on in this country, but let me tell him that to my mind there is no one so much in need of censure for his lack of doing what he ought to do for the live stock industry as the Minister of Agriculture.

maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: As to what?

maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: For not doing anything with the amount of money which is spent on the department over which the minister presides.

maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Will my hon.
friend enumerate some of the things I have not done that I should have done? I am asking the question seriously.

maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: You are doing a lot in the matter of grading, it is true. You are appointing graders and inspectors, not for beef cattle, it may be, but for hogs for the convenience of the packing companies. You have inspectors in all the packing plants to grade the intake and there is not a pound of bacon passing out of them that you have any check or control over as to grade. The government have been spending enormous sums of money in grading for the benefit of the packers.

maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is nonsense absolutely.

maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The minister says it is nonsense but let me tell him that he cannot sit there and say things of that kind. Let him, first of all, look at the records in his own department and he will find that the lower grades have been in a tremendous majority while the selects form a very small percentage indeed and no attempt has been made to grade the output of the packing companies. And the same thing applies n-ow with regard to wheat and eggs and many other things which the department is grading. What percentage of the eggs produced in this country are paid for on the bas;s of extras or extra specials? A trifling quantity. Yet the packer has taken advantage of what the government are doing and reaping the benefits from the grading along this line. The same thing happens in regard to the wheat. The wheat poo1! in t'he west I believe is endeavouring to secure the control of their wheat until it is placed on the market. They are endeavouring to obtain the advantages which heretofore went to those who were changing the grade of their grain after it had passed out of their control at the terminal elevators. This is what the Minister of Agriculture is doing all along the line

with an army of inspectors and graders all through the country. The department is costing 86,000,000 a year and the government is looking after the interest of those dealing in the produce of the farm rather than the farmer. They say, "Oh if the farmer would only produce -more?" What inducement is there to do so? The minister says that the winters are long and the cattle come out poor. There are thousands of farmers who are carrying on in the winter months producing the 'articles which are produced during the summer months, doing it well, it is true, under a handicap as to climate. What encouragement are they receiving from the government? All I have to do is to refer to the remarks of the Minister of Finance a year ago in this House. He said:
Why is it of advantage for Canada ta make a trade agreement with Australia? Well, the seasons in the two countries are exactly opposite. It is now summer in Canada,-the growing period; it is winter ds Australia. To-day our commission merchants have their agents throughout the country buying eggs, butter and cheese, to place in cold storage, on which they will have to pay storage charges, interest and insurance. Those carrying charges will be paid by the Canadian breaksfast table next winter. But we will be saved this burden if we can effect an economic arrangement wiith Australia whereby there will be a continual flow of these products from our sister commonwealth, while we are shipping our products to the United Kingdom.
During the months of the year when it is costly to produce in this country the minister will encourage imports from Australia and New Zealand to ship their products to Canada. Let me tell the minister that during the four months of the present year there have been upwards of 7,000,000 pounds of butter brought in as a result of the treaty made with Australia-subsequently extended to New Zealand-something that never happened in a like period before.

maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: It was more than that in 1915 and 1916.

maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I said in four months. There was never a time in the history of Canada when for a like period so much was imported.

maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh yes.

maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The minister says he is going to cheapen the cost of the breakfast table. That is apparently the object in view and not the development of agriculture. I could not help but imagine how the Americans must have smiled when they read the order in council passed by the government. "If you will only allow our cattle to have access to your market, we will do the same for you." It is the American people the minister is looking after and not

Cattle Industry
the Canadian people at all. Those who listened to the president of the United States a year ago last fa'll at the Chicago winter fair will realize that they have no intention of lowering the duty to compel the farmers of the United States to compete with imports of cattle or anything else from this country. That is not their object at all, when the president stated that if it was found that the American farmer was suffering from the competition of other countries the tariff would be increased to protect him. The American does not look upon this matter the way hon. gentlemen opposite looks upon it. In the United States they have appointed a tariff commission to look after their interests. I have here the ninth report of the tariff commission of the United States. How do they look at these matters? There they ascertain the cost of production, and the Minister of Agriculture, with his $6,000,000 annual expenditure, is not able to tell us the cost of production of a single thing grown on the farm.

maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I can tell the hon. member the cost of every one.

maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I
hope the minister will at last be able to give us this information rather than to indulge in the generalities he has indulged in to-night. What does the tariff commission of the United States say in regard to their objective? It says:
The law seeks to provide a mathematical formula for the equalization of costs of production in accordance with the provision of section 315. If, for example. the existing duty on a particular commodity does not equalize, as between the foreign and domestic manufacturer, production costs ascertained as provided in the statute, it is the function o-f the tariff commission to make investigations to assist the president to find a rate which will tend to correct the inequality.
The object they have is to ascertain the cost of production in their own country and in other countries, and if something can be produced in a foreign country cheaper than in the United States, then they put up the tariff to protect their people. I know that the matter of tariff, or the safeguarding of industries, or protection, the elimination of competition or whatever you see fit to call it, is not a popular issue with many people. Personally I would prefer to see free trade indulged in by all the countries of the world. In that case I believe we could hold our own with the best of them, but unfortunately the attitude of other countries is to increase their tariff in order to protect their own people against the imports of other countries, and we have to deal with the conditions with which we are confronted rather than with some
idea! which we may have in our mind and which we would like to see in effect.
The cattle industry of this country is undoubtedly the very foundation upon which successful agriculture must be built up, and if the cattle industry is not successful then the agricultural industry is not successful, and we may just as well brush to one side all these generalities which the Minister of Agriculture indulged in with regard to what ought to be done. One of the essentials is a better and cheaper arrangement for the transportation of live stock in this country, particularly beef and store cattle, on account of the different conditions to be found in different provinces. In some sections it is apparent that while they can raise young cattle they find some difficulty in finishing them on account of the lack of suitable accommodation as to shelter and feed. I do not believe the climatic conditions are so very difficult to overcome, but I do realize that with the costs of tronsportation for short hauls in the old provinces, which have been not only doubled but nearly trebled in the last twenty years, great difficulties are encountered. We have not as good a rate for shipment of live stock as is enjoyed by the shippers of many other commodities. This is a matter that ought to be pressed as forcibly as possible upon the Board of Railway Commissioners, in order that better rates may be given for the transportation of cattle than now obtain. The United States market is undoubtedly a good one. When we realize that despite their high tariff against our cattle, immense numbers are still being shipped across the line, we fully appreciate what we lost when they raised the tariff against importations from Canada. That, however, is their business and it is something that we cannot force them to give way on.
Nevertheless we are in a most favourable position by reason of the fact that in all this northern country, northern Ontario, northern Quebec, British Columbia, while the Americans to-day practically control the greatest proportion of our pulp lands and many of our water-powers, and they are taking our raw material in immense quantities across the line to manufacture them over there. It is our duty to look after our people and their interests and if we do that in a scientific way we can very quickly obtain these concessions from the United States instead of going begging to them, as the minister apparently has 'been doing and saying: Oh, if you will only remove the tariff off our cattle we will remove our tariff on yours, or something that it is immaterial to you
Cattle Industry

whether we remove it or not. You will never obtain anything by methods of that kind.
This is one of the most important questions that can come before parliament. It is something that has been before parliament ever since we met this session. But instead of the government doing something along the line advocated by the hon. member for Macleod, there has been a constant knocking, knocking of agriculture from the beginning to the present by encouraging the importation of agricultural products from countries where they can be produced more cheaply than in Canada. The minister steps down now and says that the blame is on all those farmers who produce this inferior stock and tells them to produce better stock. Only two years ago he was predicting that the day would come when stores would be opened in the large cities of this country retailing the agricultural products of Australia and New Zealand. Since that time he has removed what little protection we had against importations which were then coming in from those countries. Only three or four weeks before the last general election an order in council was put through on the quiet, without publicity, and the same concessions which had been granted to Australia were extended to New Zealand. I placed a motion on the order paper asking for the correspondence which had taken place. Was there any correspondence on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture with the government of New Zealand in regard to why those concessions should be granted? There was not a scratch of the pen to show that any correspondence had taken place between the two governments or any members of the government. The government granted those concessions to New Zealand without obtaining anything in return from the sister dominion, although it maintains a high protective tariff against us.
Why was this done? The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) stated this year: Oh, we were afraid they were going to raise the tariff on newsprint and paper; that is the reason why we granted the concessions to New Zealand and sacrificed the interest of agriculture. These concessions were not asked for by New Zealand, but the government granted them under pressure from somebody, not those engaged in agriculture, and I defy the Minister of Agriculture to show where, since he has been minister, he has shown that he has had the interests of agriculture at heart and that he has not given way to those engaged in some other occupation to gratify their desires.

Oh, but he will say, we got the British embargo removed from Canadian cattle. It is true that the embargo was removed while this government was in office, but the hon. gentleman sitting in front of me, the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers) was the man who started that matter and who secured from the British government a promise that the embargo would be removed. This was under pressure, because the British people believe in carrying out their promises, and they adopted this policy not on account of any disease amongst our cattle but as a means of protecting their farmers, because they have a protective policy just as much as any other country in the world. That was the reason why they put that embargo into effect and when they were charged with breach of faith with those to whom they had made the promise they realized that it was up to them to remove the embargo. The embargo, I will admit, was removed while the minister was in office, and he wants to carry off all the glory for having had it removed.

speechtext:
I have always
given my predecessors every credit.

maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: The minister took good care to-night to claim all the credit he could for it.

maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I did not.

maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I did not hear him give his predecessors much credit for what was done along that line. I have a list of the imports of agricultural products and it is really startling to leam that a country with such immense agricultural possibilities as we have should be importing such large quantities of agricultural products. This goes to show the effect of a policy such as we have in this country where the government are not protecting the people but are allowing surplus products from other countries to come in at certain times when the cost of production is high so as to destroy the market absolutely. The result is that the farmers become discouraged and say: Well, if that is the kind of treatment we are to receive we will go out of business. People can go out of business more easily than they can stay in an unprofitable business, and that is the reason why they are going across the line just as fast to-day as they ever were.
I was bom in this country; I have been engaged in agriculture all my life, and I have been hopeful that the great possibilities of agriculture in Canada would eventually be realized and that we would obtain the full

Safeguarding of hidustries
advantage to which we are naturally entitled. But I must confess that as the days and the years pass I have reached the conclusion that if the present policy is to be continued and applied to agriculture, all I can say is: God help those who are engaged in agriculture in Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: If the hon. member for Macleod exercises the privilege of replying he closes the debate. If any other hon. member desires to speak he should do so now.

maintopic: CATTLE INDUSTRY MOTION FOR SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I would like to make only one or two remarks before closing the debate. The first is in regard to a statement made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) that it is unfortunate that this motion did not come up earlier in the session. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, I would have
11 p.m. been glad to have it come up much earlier in the session, but unfortunately the government took most of the private members' days since the beginning of the session and if my memory serves me aright we have so far only had four Mondays as private members' days. I hope that in later sessions of this parliament the government will not need to take private members' days; that they will find some method of improving the rules of the House so that we shall not have debates on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne lasting six weeeks and budget debates lasting five weeks. If this parliament is to function as a legislative body it is necessary that some change in the rules should be made. I do not want to get away from the question under discussion to debate the rules of the House, but during the last three months I have sat here very impatiently wondering if we would ever get down to business.
I am going to accept the suggestion of the Minister of Agriculture, and if the House will permit I will ask the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Jelliff) to move an amendment asking that this matter be referred to the select standing committee on Agriculture and Colonization. Before I sit down I would like to say just one word in regard to the question raised by the Minister of Agriculture who cannot understand why the farmers of Canada do not produce more cattle for the British market. As I pointed out to him this afternoon in my remarks, the steer that the farmer does produce now for export brings him only 50 per cent of the purchasing power of 1913,
and he was not making any inordinate profit then. That is the reason why we are asking for this committee to-day. I hope my good friend from Lethbridge will now move an amendment asking that this matter be referred to the standing committee on Agriculture.
