speakeroldname: Mr. A. E. ROSS (Kingston City) moved:
speechtext:
That in the opinion of this House our industries here have to have safeguarding with respect to competition from other parts of tlhe worM, competition from the country to the south, competition from conditions as they are in Europe.
He said: Mr. Speaker, at this late hour I shall shorten my remarks as much as possible on this very important subject and confine myself to the discussion of three main features: first, the relation of the membere of this House to t'he resolution; second, the relation of Canada to other countries in regard to this resolution; third, the relation of this resolution to one of the great problems of this country. In addition I shall deal with two or three special features.
If I had been at a loss for a reason for introducing this resolution, I would have found a very good one in the speech by the hon. member for Huron (Mr. McMillan). The tenor of his speech was-if you could only gain an entrance into the markets of the country to the south, wihat a fine thing it would be for us. In a way it was a wail, the expression of a lost hope, of an anticipation that he did not see possible of realization. I would recall to 'his memory the words of his former leader, who some years ago laid down thB policy of himself and his party that they would no longer "make pilgrimages to Washington." We are also reminded of the futility of such pilgrimages by the remarks expressed to-day in this House about looking to Washington for the solution of another question of great importance to this country. Pilgrimages to Washington have been failures in the past, and I would remind my hon.

Safeguarding of Industries

friend from Huron that they will lead to failure in the future.
Members in all quarters of this House have talked of protection, calling it 'by such terms as encouragement of industry, safeguarding of industry, and so on. This resolution now desires the opinion of the House on the question of safeguarding Canadian industry from all forms of competition. The appointment of a tariff board does not eliminate the necessity for such a resolution. Its discussion will give everybody in this House an opportunity of expressing opinions such as they have voiced on many occasions in the past. The position set forth in the resolution is one taken and maintained by this party throughout all the years of its history since Sir John A. Macdonald introduced the National Policy. The resolution should also secure the support of many of our friends on the opposite side, if they could but give expression to their real feelings. They should have no hesitation in supporting the policy I have outlined because their leader has on more than one occasion expressed himself fully in accord with it. In fact when I have quoted several remarks by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) it will be found that this resolution is in language he has used on several occasions. At Erindale in September of last year the Mail and Empire reports him as follows:
He stood for a tariff to give us what we need in the way of revenue and at the same time to safeguard industrial development.
At Fort William in October he made use of these words:
We do not want to work injury to any industry. We want to help as far as possible all industries.
During the campaign he had occasion to come to Kingston and give a lengthy address in an attempt to win over the city. The position taken by the right hon. gentleman on that occasion, as reported by the British Whig, was as follows:
We have decided to form a board to consider all tariff schedules, and to call for advice to the board representatives of manufacturing, of commerce, of agriculture, cf labour, and also of the women so that the homes would be dealt with fairly. The government widl take final action because the power of taxation cannot be given to a non-responsible body. The desire was to help every industry-
These are his own words:
The desrire was to help every industry, and the one aim was to establish them. His government was not in favour of free trade, it never was, never would be. There must be protection against competition.
Those are his words?

Those are the
words of the Prime Minister quoted from the party's own paper, the British Whig of King-
ston. I have also a quotation from the same speech as reported by the London Advertiser. No one on the other side can offer any objection to a quotation from that paper. Its language is contained in the resolution, and is the language used by the right hon. Prime Minister in the city of Kingston that same evening. This is what he then said:
We realize that our industries here have to have safeguarding with respect to competition from other parts of the world, competition from the country to the south, competition from conditions as they are in Europe.
So there is no member on the other side but can find good reason for supporting this resolution when it is coubhed in the words of their own leader. The Mail and Empire contained this report:
The city of Kingston need have no fear from a Liberal administration as to the well-being of its industries. The industries would be taken care of.
Whose words were those?

The same speech made by the Prime Minister in Kingston. Taking their cue from the Prime Minister, all hon. members opposite should be in favour of this resolution.
The next point is the relation of this country to other countries in regard to this resolution. I am not going to dwell very long upon this, because it has been repeatedly mentioned in the House during other debates. There are one or two new features, however, to which I would like to draw the attention of the House. As has already been said, every country with any degree of prosperity has adopted some method of safeguarding industries, but our friends across the border have some new ideas in addition to the strong stand they have taken. At present they have a board of survey making an examination of the articles manufactured in Canada, to see if they can stimulate the manufacture of the same articles in the United States and so obviate the necessity of importing them from Canada. They have also certain treasury agents in France whose actions are being complained of by French manufacturers. These agents are investigating the cost of manufacturing goods, so that the goods will be brought into the United States at a proper valuation and not at some fictitious figure given by the manufacturer. These two features show the attitude of the United States in preventing interference with their industries.
I have a long article here dealing with the work of David Syme in Australia. I am not going to read it at this late hour, but I would like to draw attention to the conclusion of

Safeguarding of Industries
the article. David Syme founded the colony of Victoria under a policy of free trade. The gold mines had brought a large population to Victoria, but the mines failed, and the population of about one million were left in idleness and almost destitute. David Syme immediately initiated a policy of protection, and succeeded in having the raw products of Victoria manufactured in that country. It is very interesting to study the results; he found that a nation of specialists, whether of farmers or importers or manufacturers, did not supply the requisite and fundamentally necessary condition of permanency which can only be supplied by a society of varied enterprises and multifarious employments. So he inaugurated a policy by which the raw products of Victoria should be manufactured in the colony, rather than brought in from the outside.
Let us consider what was accomplished. Side by side with the colony of Victoria was founded the colony of New South Wales. That colony also had a policy of free trade and a policy of bonused immigration, which Victoria did not adopt. In comparing the two colonies, in 1922-23 the manufacturing industries of New South Wales numbered 6,072, while those of Victoria numbered 7,096. In 1919 New South Wales had employed 144,454 persons, while Victoria only employed 136,522 people. But in 1923, four years after this new policy was inaugurated, New South Wales had employed 152,266 while Victoria had reached the same number. But when it came to the density of population, notwithstanding the fact that New South Wales had brought thousands of immigrants into the country by means of bonuses, the density of population there was 7.14, while in Victoria it was 18.49. These figures will immediately prove that the policy of initiating and safeguarding industries has brought excellent results in Victoria.
Another point I wanted to bring to the attention of the House is that this resolution has a very intimate relation to one of the greatest problems facing us to-day, that of immigration. During the debates which have taken place in this House this session I think every person has come to the conclusion that we require population, and that population will solve all our difficulties. Increased population will lessen our taxes and relieve the railway situation, and I want to demonstrate how this resolution affects that great problem. This government, along with other governments, has been on the wrong track altogether in their attempts to make Canada prosperous. We are at present directing all our efforts 14011-2484
in immigration to bringing into this country farmers and farm labourers. Never in the history of the world has a policy of this kind, the restriction of immigration efforts to the bringing in of agriculturists, produced any great increase in population. If I can prove that point I think I can bring every member of this House to look favourably upon this resolution. The only occasions when population rapidly increased were when some impetus was given to industrial development, and I believe that if we study the history of the world we will find that that has been the case in every country where such a rapid increase has come about.
It has been said that population is the wealth of a country; without population there can be no wealth. Colorado was a desert in 1858, but in 1890 the property of Colorado was valued at $239,000,000. So it was with the Cobalt district and so with the Yukon and many other places; without population there can be no wealth. On the other hand, as another illustration let me refer to the valley of the Amazon. Here is perhaps the richest country in the world, with great natural resources, but with a very sparse population. On the other hand, in the island of Barbados, you find great wealth and a large population. Population is the secret of wealth. The instances I have given prove that population is necessary for the production of wealth in any country. On the other hand, no state can support a lot of unproductive consumers. The prosperous state is that where there is population and the wealth, the country where you have population, and work for the people. There are a lot of countries where there is density of population but not wealth. Take China, for instance, and some parts of India. The secret is this:	Population and work must go hand
in hand.
While we all recognize that agriculture is our basic industry, it cannot give us that increase of population of which Canada stands very much in need at the present time. All increase of population has been due, as I said before, to an impetus in industrial development. Let me take a few countries for the sake of illustration. In the fourteenth, fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, the population of England and Wales was almost stationary. There were forty-two towns with a population of 168,000 and thirty-eight counties with a population of 1.200,000, making with Durham, Chester and Wales a total population of about 2,250,000. London had a population of only 35,000; York, 11,000; Bristol 9,500. There were no other places with a
Safeguarding of Industries

population of over 5,000, but in 1690 a hearth tax that was taken showed that the population had doubled, just by natural and other causes. Now agriculture, which was the chief industry, had made no advance. Whatever growth there had been was due to the introduction of weavers and textile workers, and their industries, from the continent.
Now jump from that period of three or four centuries without any growth in population to the period from 1831 to 1896. The population of England and other countries showed a great increase in that period. The population of England increased from 24,000,000 in 1831 to 39,500,000 in 1896; Germany, from
29.000.	000 to 52,000,000; Russia, from 58,000,000 to 105,000,000; the United States from
9.000.	000 to 70,000,000, or an increase of 626 per cent. What were the reasons for that great growth?-and here we get the proof that development along agricultural lines alone will not give us the population we require. There were different causes for that rapid growth in population in all these countries during the period from 1831 to 1896? The tremendous jump in the Russian population was largely due to the granting of the freedom of the serfs. These serfs, who had been retained on the farms, when set free entered the towns. There was a real townward tendency at that time, and the population of the cities went up. With the better conditions of the serfs, the growth of population was very rapid.
But that did not account for the rapid increase in population in the other countries. In these other countries it was due to certain other factors, one of which was the introduction of steam. The use of steam led to a great growth in railways, steamships, trade and commerce, manufactures, and in the use of manufactured agricultural implements. There followed a great industrial development, and there was in consequence a rapid growth in population. At the end of that period we find that the'number of towns with a population of 50,000 were as follows:
In 1831 there were 85 towns and cities in Europe with a population of 50,000; in the United States, 4; in the colonies, none. In 1891 there were 255 towns in Europe with a population of 50,000; 56 in the United States;
9 in the colonies. In this period of sixty years, the cities throughout practically the whole world showed an increase of population of 470 per cent, while the population outside the cities rose only 70 per cent; agriculture rose 110 per cent; and manufacturing 800 per cent.
My object in quoting these figures is to prove that the impetus given to industrial

development is the only means for giving that increase of population which is desired in this country, and the rapid increase in population which I have mentioned in these various countries was due to the causes I have given 

the discovery of steam principally, and other powers. In 1831 there were hand powers, 23,400; horse powers, 93,900; steam powers,
6,000.	In 1896 those figures had increased to hand powers, 38,000; horse powers, 179,000; and steam powers, 222,000, showing a terrific growth in the development of horse and steam power, due to the discovery and the use of steam. Manufacturing was advancing in every way, and commerce was building up large coast cities.
Just a word in regard to France. The growth in France did not come up to the measure of England and the other countries for the reason-and this will strengthen my argument- that in those days France was obtaining her manufactured products from other countries. She was getting woollens from Spain, linens from Holland, and silks from Italy. But about the year 1800 France began to wake up to her situation at that time, and saw that she was being a hewer of wood and a drawer of water for other countries, and so she set about developing her manufactures, and the result was that her population increased rapidly. There are many figures that would prove it, but I think the figures I have already given will prove that the attitude we are taking as a country to-day in lending all our efforts to the development of the industry of agriculture alone, great as that industry is, will not give us the population we require unless we attend also to the development of our other industries. Watchfulness, wakefulness, a careful attitude towards industry-this is what has made the difference in all countries. Take Scotland and Ireland, which are equal in population. The former country is estimated to be 60 per cent richer on account of the greater development of industrial work. Spain without any industry is thinly populated; Italy is thickly populated, but both countries are poor. Belgium has the maximum density of population and Sweden has the smallest density of any country in the world, yet both these countries are rich. What is the secret? The secret is population and work. You have population in Italy without industrial development. In Spain you have want of work and want of population. In Sweden you have a minimum population but a very active industrial life and consequently a rich country. Belgium is thickly populated and there the industrial and the agricultural life is very active. The density of population is the maximum of the

Safeguarding of Industries
entire world and, what is more important, the emigration from that nation is the smallest of any country.
By our careless and indifferent attitude towards our industries we have been left in the position w'e are in to-day. Without going back for any extended period let us take the population Canada has lost in the years 1924 and 1925. In 1924 the loss of population was
148.000	and in 1925 it was 111,000. Not only have we lost this amount of population but we have lost a revenue of S18 per head which that population represented. Wh have actually thrown $4,680,000 into the coffers of the United States in addition to permitting an exodus of
260.000	people to take place to that country. And that exodus is still continuing. The statement that Canadians are now returning from the United States does not impress me. They are going from Canada at a faster rate than they are returning. The port of Kingston is passing out an average of 25 a week. The staff of the American consulate in Toronto has again been increased in order to cope with the exodus from Canada. Therefore we are not in a very prosperous condition. It is evident when thousands are still leaving the country that we have not adopted a policy that will give us population.
Now, what relation has population to this question? If we adopted an actual, active policy of safeguarding Canadian industries what would it mean in regard to the population of this country? I will explain the method I adopted in order to answer that question. We are importing into this country millions of dollars of manufactured goods. I have taken the figures representing those imports and I have gone to the industries in Canada which manufacture the same class of articles, and have inquired whether these goods could be produced in Canada. In every case, in connection with the figures which I am about to give, the answer returned has been "we can". Translate that importation of manufactured goods into labour in this country and see what it will mean to Canada in the way of population. Last year we imported in round numbers cotton goods to the value of $34,000,000. I went to Dominion Textiles and said to them: "You manufacture these goods. How many people could t you employ in Canada every day in the year, all year round, if you manufactured these imported articles?" They answered. "Seven thousand." So that if these goods brought in last year were manufactured in Canada we would be able to give employment to 7,000 more people in this country.
Now, as to printed material. The importations last year amounted to $12,000,000. I went to some of our people who are engaged
in printing and sgtid to them: "If these purchases were made in Canada what would it mean in the way of labour?" Their answer was that it would give employment to 4,000 people. We imported engines to the value of $11,600,000. If these were manufactured in Canada they would give employment to 4,200 people. Of machinery there is $30,200,000 worth imported. If manufactured in Canada they would give employment t.o 10,000 people. Wearing apparel to the amount of $6,350,000 was imported. The manufacture in Canada would employ 3,000 people. Of cloth, yam. blankets, rugs, and felts, we imported $35,000,000. The manufacture of these articles in Canada would give work to 18,500 people. We imported vehicles to the amount of $36,400,009. If made in Canada they would give employment to 8,000 people. We brought in leather goods to the value of $7,324,000. If they were made in this country, 2,500 people would be employed. The importation of farm implements represented $11,200,000. Their manufacture in this country would keep 3,000 people busy. Our importations of paper amounted to $9,100,000. If the manufacturing were carried on in this Dominion it would mean employment for 1,800 persons. Taking the foregoing ten branches of industry the manufacture of goods to the amount given would mean employment for 73,700 people in Canada, or taking four as the average number to a family, an addition to our population of approximatly 280,000 persons. We have spent $3,000,000 a year on immigration. If you safeguard our industries you can add 280,000 people to our population and save that expenditure of $3,000,000 yearly. Apply the same argument to other lines of industry such as electrical apparatus, gas apparatus, explosives, furniture, matches, fibre ware, mouldings, and amusement and sporting goods. If you put into operation a thorough and active policy with respect to them you will have no fear as to the future of this country and its growth of population.
There are one or two other points to which I wish to draw attention. We are actually lying down on the job of developing two of the greatest industries that any country could have, with almost illimitable possibilities. I refer to the working of our ores, and along with that the development of a chemical industry. We need to-day encouragement enough to produce still another Consolidated Smelters, to be located in eastern Canada. Study for a moment what that great industry means to British Columbia. By a policy of working our own ores a return has been brought to that province from two or three
Safeguarding of Industries

mines amounting in the case of silver to $3,105,000, in the case of lead to $20,066,630, in the case of copper, to $4,763,707, and in the case of zinc, to $36,012,600. The development of these ores from two or three mines only in that province has produced a wealth such as I have described. In fact, it takes your breath away when you think of what this country could do if the government would come to life, wake up to the immense possibilities of this country and put in operation a policy that would develop them. Along with that goes the development of the chemist. You cannot work on ores without connecting them up with the chemical industry, and no other industry in the world will store up as much wealth if it is properly protected and its development is placed in the hands of experts. We have everything in this country that would produce as valuable a chemical industry as that which flourishes in the United States or anywhere else.
In addition to these rich ores that we have -and I have only given the House an example of what two or three mines in British Columbia will do-a great development is going on now up in the Rouyn area, in the new field w'here zinc, copper and lead ores, which we have not touched in the east before, are being discovered. Hon. members will realize that if this government would only become alive to the interests of the country, or get off the job and let the Progressives take charge, they might develop one industry at least and increase the wealth of this country. But I am surprised that even the Progressives have not pointed out the fact that we have non-metallic products in this country. Some person came down from the west and tried to interest the government in Epsom salts. Perhaps they thought it would be a good thing to give them, but they are not even interested in that. Along with that salt you have the importation of household salt, with immense fields in this country, of phosphates and sulphate of soda. You have also the graphite industry. The pencils that are used in the House of Commons are United States pencils, made with United States graphite, whereas there is a very large supply of graphite in Canada. The field for graphite in this country, however, is lying idle for want of interest, and productive development is not taking place.
It has been pointed out that this government does not keep alive to the development of the country. I might draw attention to the fact that in the county of Frontenac there is the only field of feldspar on the American con-
[Air. A. E. Ross.]
tinent. Canada has now undertaken the grinding of that feldspar. There is a factory in the city of Kingston and one in Toronto, yet this government it sitting idly by and seeing the feldspar taken out of this country, sent over to the United States, ground in the factories there, and brought back to Canada as ground feldspar. With those two industries trying to compete in a situation such as that, it is deplorable that the government, with their experts in the Department of Mines, should take no action. Just imagine; we have a Department of Mines, which has repeatedly, by reports from experts, brought before the government the importance of the development of these ores and non-metallic substances, but no action is taken. The feldspar still goes out of the country. In 1924 we brought into Canada 1,661 tons of our ground feldspar while at the same time we had two mills of our own. In 1925 we brought back 1,712 tons of this ground feldspar.
I have coupled up with the subject of industry, perhaps, matters that have not been taken up before, because I tried to cover a new field, and to emphasize the fact that the safeguarding of our industries, agricultural and manufacturing, the development of our ores and of the chemical industry, would produce in this country a population such as we desire and such as we are not obtaining, in spite of the fact that we are spending $3,000,000 a year upon immigration.
In conclusion, I point out that the safeguarding of our industries will produce a settled permanent population. Just imagine the economic loss to this country and to the world at large when the policy introduced by this government closes up mills in Canada and sends the population of workmen away I What does it mean? It means that these people must get employment in some other country, and the unfortunate part of it is that if they do not go out of the country they must begin to fit themselves for some other employment and so interfere with those already engaged in that employment. It is an economic loss any way you look at it, owing to the carelessness and the indifference of the government in regard to the industrial development of the country, whether it be agriculture or otherwise. If* industry is looked after, watchfully handled and taken care of in the manner adopted by other countries, it will give us a permanent population.
I have endeavoured to-night in dealing with this question to keep to the four points I set out to discuss; first the relation of the members of this House, including the Prime

Minister, to the safeguarding of industries; second, the relation of Canada, in comparison with the other countries of the world, to the safeguarding of industry; third, the relation of this resolution to the great policy of population, which will be the panacea for all our troubles, and fourth, the special features to which I have referred. We have listened this afternoon and this evening to discussions on wheat in relation to cattle and during that discussion topics of all sorts have been brought up. But I am desirous to-night that we shall confine ourselves to this one thing, the safeguarding of industries, and I think I have proven to the House that if we would take care of the industries we have and endeavour to establish others along lines connected with our natural resources, we would in a short time save the expenditure of this $3,000,000 on immigration and have a stable, settled, happy and prosperous Canada.
